questions.text: For non-degenerately doped n-type silicon, which one of the following plots represents the temperature [latex](T)[/latex] dependence of free electron concentration [latex](n)[/latex] ?

In a semiconductor device, the Fermi-energy level is [latex]0.35 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] above the valence band energy. The effective density of states in the valence band at [latex]T=300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is [latex]1 \times 10^{19} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. The thermal equilibrium hole concentration in silicon at [latex]400 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is ___ [latex]\_\times 10^{13} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. (rounded off to two decimal places).
Given [latex]\mathrm{kT}[/latex] at [latex]300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is [latex]0.026 \mathrm{eV}[/latex].
questions.solution:
Given,
[latex] E_{F}-E_{V}=0.35 \mathrm{eV} \quad \text { [Considering it is given at } 400 \mathrm{~K} \text { ] } [/latex]
Also, [latex]V_{T_{1}}=K T_{1}=0.026 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] at [latex]T_{1}=300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] [latex]\frac{V_{T_{1}}}{V_{T_{2}}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} \Rightarrow V_{T_{2}}=\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} \times V_{T_{1}}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] [latex]V_{T_{2}}=\frac{400}{300} \times 0.026[/latex]
[latex]V_{T_{2}}=0.03466 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] at [latex]T_{2}=400 \mathrm{~K}[/latex]

Now, [latex]N_{v}=1 \times 10^{19} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}[/latex] at [latex]T_{1}=300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex]
[latex]N_{v} \propto T^{3 / 2}[/latex]
[latex]\frac{N_{V_{2}}}{N_{V_{1}}}=\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{3 / 2}[/latex]
[latex]N_{V_{2}}=\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{3 / 2} N V_{1}[/latex]
[latex]\left(\because T_{2}=400 \mathrm{~K}\right)[/latex] [latex]=\left(\frac{400}{300}\right)^{3 / 2} N_{V_{1}}[/latex]
[latex]N_{V_{2}}=1.5396 \times 10^{19} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}[/latex]

Now, hole concentration at [latex]400 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} & p=N_{V} e^{-\left(E_{F}-E_{V}\right) / k T_{2}}=1.5396 \times 10^{19} \times e^{-0.35 \mathrm{eV} / 0.03466 \mathrm{eV}} \\ & p=63.36 \times 10^{13} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned} [/latex]

questions.text:
In an extrinsic semiconductor, the hole concentration is given to be [latex]1.5 n_{i}[/latex] where [latex]n_{i}[/latex] is the intrinsic carrier concentration of [latex]1 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. The ratio of electron to hole mobility for equal hole and electron drift current is given as ___
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.solution:
Given, intrinsic carrier concentration [latex]n_{i}=1 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]
Hole concentration,
[latex]\quad p=1.5 \times n_{i}[/latex]
[latex] p=1.5 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} [/latex]

Given, electron and hole current are equal
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{p \text { dritt }} & =I_{n \text { dritt }} \\ p q \mu_{p} E A & =n q \mu_{n} E A \\ 1.5 \times 10^{10} \mu_{p} & =n \mu_{n} \quad ...(i) \end{aligned} [/latex]

But according to mass action law,
[latex] \begin{aligned} n p & =n_{i}^{2} \\ n & =\frac{n_{i}}{1.5}=\frac{10^{10}}{1.5} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Put in equation (i)
[latex]\therefore \quad 1.5 \times 10^{10} \mu_{p}=\frac{10^{10}}{1.5} \times \mu_{n}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{\mu_{n}}{\mu_{p}}=2.25 [/latex]

questions.text: For an intrinsic semiconductor at temperature [latex]T=0 \mathrm{~K}[/latex], which of the following statement is true?
options: All energy states in the valence band are filled with electrons and all energy states in the conduction band are empty of electrons.
All energy states in the valence band are empty of electrons and all energy states in the conduction band are filled with electrons.
All energy states in the valence and conduction band are filled with holes.
All energy states in the valence and conduction band are filled with electrons.
questions.solution:
Intrinsic semiconductor at [latex]\mathrm{T}=0 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] behaves as an insulator.
Hence, valence band is completely filled with electron and conduction band is completely empty.

questions.text: In a semiconductor, if the Fermi energy level lies in the conduction band, then the semiconductor is known as
questions.solution: As the Fermi lies inside the conduction band hence it is degenerate [latex]n[/latex]-type semiconductor.

questions.text: Select the CORRECT statement(s) regarding semiconductor devices.
options: Electrons and holes are of equal density in an intrinsic semiconductor at equilibrium.
Collector region is generally more heavily doped than Base region in a BJT.
Total current is spatially constant in a two terminal electronic device in dark under steady state condition.
Mobility of electrons always increases with temperature in Silicon beyond 300 K.
questions.solution:
At equilibrium [latex]n = p = n_i[/latex] for intrinsic semiconductor
Collector region is generally lightly doped then base region in BJT. Hence option B is wrong.
By increasing temperature above 300K, mobality of electrons decreases hence option (D) is also wrong

questions.text: In a non-degenerate bulk semiconductor with electron density [latex]n=10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex], the value of [latex]E_C-E_{Fn}=200meV[/latex], where [latex]E_C[/latex] and [latex]E_{Fn}[/latex] denote the bottom of the conduction band energy and electron Fermi level energy, respectively. Assume thermal voltage as 26 meV and the intrinsic carrier concentration is [latex]10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex]. For [latex]n=0.5 \times 10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex], the closest approximation of the value of ([latex]E_C-E_{Fn}[/latex]), among the given options, is ______.
questions.solution:
Here we have to find the value of [latex]E_c-E_{fn}[/latex]
As we know,
[latex]E_C-E_F=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n} \right ) \;\;\;...(i)[/latex]
[latex]E_C-E_{F1}=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n_1} \right ) \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
[latex]E_C-E_{F2}=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n_2} \right ) \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
Equation (ii) - Equation (iii)
[latex](E_C-E_{F1})-(E_C-E_{F2})=kT \ln \left ( \frac{\frac{N_c}{n_1}}{\frac{N_c}{n_2}} \right )=kT \ln \frac{n_2}{n_1}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow 200meV-(E_C-E_{F2})=26meV \times \ln \left ( \frac{0.5 \times 10^{16}}{1 \times 10^{16}} \right )[/latex]
[latex] 200meV-(E_C-E_{F2})=+26meV \ln (0.5)=-18[/latex]
[latex](E_C-E_{F2})=200+8=218meV[/latex]

questions.text: Consider a long rectangular bar of direct bandgap p-type semiconductor. The equilibrium hole density is [latex]10^{17}cm^{-3}[/latex] and the intrinsic carrier concentration is [latex]10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex]. Electron and hole diffusion lengths are [latex]2\mu m[/latex]and [latex]1\mu m[/latex], respectively. The left side of the bar ([latex]x=0[/latex]) is uniformly illuminated with a laser having photon energy greater than the bandgap of the semiconductor. Excess electron-hole pairs are generated ONLY at [latex]x=0[/latex] because of the laser. The steady state electron density at [latex]x=0[/latex] is [latex]10^{14}cm^{-3}[/latex]  due to laser illumination. Under these conditions and ignoring electric field, the closest approximation (among the given options) of the steady state electron density at [latex]x=2 \mu m[/latex], is _____
questions.solution:
From continuity equation of electrons
[latex]\frac{dn}{dt}=n\mu _n\frac{dE}{dx}+\mu _nE\frac{dn}{dx}+G_n-R_n+x_n\frac{d^2x}{dx^2} \;\;\;...(i)[/latex]
[Because [latex]\vec{E}[/latex] is not mentioned hence
[latex]\frac{dE}{dx}=0[/latex]
For [latex] x \gt 0, G_n[/latex] is also zero
[latex]n=\frac{n_i^2}{N_A}=\frac{10^{20}}{10^{17}}=10^3[/latex]
[latex]n=n_0+\delta n=10^3+10^{14}=10^{14}[/latex]
at steady state, [latex]\frac{db}{dt}=0[/latex]
Hence equation (i) becomes:
[latex]O=D_n\frac{d^2\delta n}{dx^2}-\frac{\delta n}{\tau _n}[/latex]
[latex]\frac{d^2\delta n}{dx^2}=\frac{\delta n}{L_n^2} \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
From solving equation (ii)
[latex]\delta _n(x)=\delta _n(0)e^{-x/L_n}[/latex]
at [latex]x=2\mu m[/latex]
[latex]\delta _n(2\mu m)=10^{14}e^{-2/2}=10^{14}e^{-1}=0.37 \times 10^{14}[/latex]

questions.text:
The energy band diagram of a p-type semiconductor bar of length L under equilibrium condition (i.e.. the Fermi energy level [latex]E_{F}[/latex] is constant) is shown in the figure. The valance band [latex]E_{V}[/latex] is sloped since doping is non-uniform along the bar. The difference between the energy levels of the valence band at the two edges of the bar is [latex]\Delta[/latex].

If the charge of an electron is q, then the magnitude of the electric field developed inside this semiconductor bar is
questions.solution:
The built-in electric field is due to non-uniform doping (the semiconductor is under equilibrium)


[latex]\begin{aligned} E &=\frac{1}{q}\frac{ d E_{v}}{d x} \\ &=\frac{1}{q} \frac{\Delta}{L} \\ &=\frac{\Delta}{q L} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A bar of silicon is doped with boron concentration of [latex]10^{16} \text{cm}^{-3}[/latex]  and assumed to be fully ionized. It is exposed to light such that electron-hole pairs are generated throughout the volume of the bar at the rate of [latex]10^{20} \text{cm}^{-3} s^{-1}[/latex]. If the recombination lifetime is [latex]100 \;\mu s[/latex], intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon is [latex]10^{10} \text{cm}^{-3}[/latex] and assuming [latex]100\%[/latex] ionization of boron, then the approximate product of steady-state electron and hole concentrations due to this light exposure is
questions.solution:
Boron [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Acceptor type doping


[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{A} &=10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \\ g_{0 p} &=1020 \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \\ \tau &=100 \mu \mathrm{s} \\ n_{i} &=10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Product of steady state electron-hole concentration =?
At thermal equilibrium (before shining light)
[latex] \begin{array}{ll} \text { Hole concentration, } & p_{o} \simeq N_{A}=10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \\ \text { Electron concentration, } & n_{0}=\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{p_{0}}=\frac{10^{20}}{10^{16}}=10^{4} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{array}[/latex]
After, illumination of light,
Hole concentration, [latex]p=p_{o}+\delta p[/latex]
Electron concentration, [latex]\quad n=n_{o}+\delta n[/latex]
Due to shining light, excess carrier concentration,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta p &=\delta n=g_{o p} \cdot \tau=10^{20} \times 100 \times 10^{-6}=10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \\ \therefore \qquad p &=10^{16}+10^{16}=2 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}\\ n&=10^{4}+10^{16} \simeq 10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, product of steady state electron-hole concentration
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=n p=10^{16} \times 2 \times 10^{16} \\ &=2 \times 10^{32} \mathrm{~cm}^{-6} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A single crystal intrinsic semiconductor is at a temperature of 300 K with effective density of states for holes twice that of electrons. The thermal voltage is 26 mV. The intrinsic Fermi level is shifted from mid-bandgap energy level by
questions.solution:
[latex]\frac{E_{c}+E_{v}}{2}-E_{F_{i}}=\frac{KT}{2}\ln \left ( \frac{N_{C}}{N_{V}}\right )\, \, \, \, \, \, \left ( \because N_{C}=\frac{N_{V}}{2} \right )[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{0.026}{2}\ln 0.5=-9.01\, meV[/latex]

questions.text: As shown a uniformly doped Silicon (Si) bar of length L = 0.1 [latex]\mu[/latex]m with a donor concentration [latex]N_{D}=10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] is illuminated at x = 0 such that electron and hole pairs are generated at the rate of [latex]G_{L}=G_{L0}(1-\frac{x}{L} ), 0 \leq x \leq L [/latex], where [latex] G_{L0}=10^{17} cm^{-3}s^{-1}[/latex]. Hole lifetime is [latex]10^{-4}s[/latex], electronic charge [latex]q=1.6\times 10^{-19}C[/latex], hole diffusion coefficient [latex]D_{P}=100 cm^{2}/s[/latex] and low level injection condition prevails. Assuming a linearly decaying steady state excess hole concentration that goes to 0 at x = L, the magnitude of the diffusion current density at x = L/2, in [latex]A/cm^{2}[/latex], is _________.
questions.solution:
Net hole density varying in the direction of x is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{n}(x) &=p_{n 0}+\Delta p=p_{n 0}+G_{L} \tau_{p} \\ &=p_{n 0}+G_{L o} \tau_{p}\left(1-\frac{x}{L}\right) \\ J_{p, \text { diff }} &=-e D_{p} \frac{d p}{d x}=-e D_{p}\left[\frac{-G_{L o} \tau_{p}}{L}\right] \\ &=\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 100 \times 10^{17} \times 10^{-4}}{0.1 \times 10^{-4}} \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \\ &=16 \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The dependence of drift velocity of electrons on electric field in a semiconductor is shown below. The semiconductor has a uniform electron concentration of [latex]n=1\times 10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] and electronic charge [latex]q=1.6\times 10^{-19}C[/latex]. If a bias of 5V is applied across a 1 [latex]\mu[/latex]m region of this semiconductor, the resulting current density in this region, in [latex]kA/cm^{2}[/latex], is _________.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} E&=\frac{V}{d}=\frac{5}{10^{-4}}=5 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{cm}\\ &\text{Slope of the curve,}\\ m &=\frac{10^{7}-0}{5 \times 10^{5}}=20 \quad y=m_{x} \\ v_{d} &=20 \times E=20 \times 5 \times 10^{4} \\ &=10^{6} \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{cm} \\ J &=n e v_{d} \\ &=1 \times 10^{16} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{6} \\ &=1.6 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}=1.6 \mathrm{kA} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A bar of Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) is doped with Silicon such that the Silicon atoms occupy Gallium and Arsenic sites in the GaAs crystal. Which one of the following statement is true?
options: Silicon atoms act as p-type dopants in Arsenic sites and n-type dopants in Gallium sites
Silicon atoms act as n-type dopants in Arsenic sites and p-type dopants in Gallium sites
Silicon atoms act as p-type dopants in Arsenic as well as Gallium sites
Silicon atoms act as n-type dopants in Arsenic as well as Gallium sites
questions.solution:
Si acts as p-type dopant GA sites.
Si acts as n-type dopant GA sites.

questions.text:
Consider a silicon sample at T = 300 K, with a uniform donor density [latex]N_{d}=5 \times 10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] illuminated uniformly such that the optical generation rate is [latex]G_{opt}=1.5 \times 10^{20}cm^{-3}s^{-1}[/latex] throughout the sample. The incident radiation is turned off at t = 0. Assume low-level injection to be valid and ignore surface effects. The carrier lifetimes are [latex]\tau _{p0}=0.1 \mu s \; and \; \tau _{n0}=0.5\mu s[/latex]

The hole concentration at t = 0 and the hole concentration at t= 0.3 [latex]\mu[/latex]s, respectively, are
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given}quad G_{opt} &=1.5 \times 10^{20} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} / \mathrm{sec} \\ G_{opt} &=R=\frac{N_{A}}{\tau_{P}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1.5 \times 10^{2} &=\frac{N_{A}}{0.1 \times 10^{-6}} \\ \therefore\quad N_{A} &=1.5 \times 10^{13} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} \\ P(t) &=P_{n0} e^{-t / \tau_{p}} \\ &=1.5 \times 10^{13} e^{\frac{-0.3}{0.1}} \\ &=7.46 \times 10^{11} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The figure below shows the doping distribution in a p-type semiconductor in log scale. The magnitude of the electric field (in kV/cm) in the semiconductor due to non uniform doping is _________
questions.solution:
Applying the current density equation
[latex] \begin{aligned} J&=J_{\text {Dritt }}+J_{\text {Diff }} \\ J&=0\\ 0 &=-q D_{p} \frac{d p}{d x}+q\mu_{p} p E \\ q D_{p} \frac{d p}{d x} &=a \mu_{p} p E \\ E &=\frac{V_{T}}{p(x)} \frac{\partial p}{d r} \\ \therefore \quad |E| &=\frac{V_{T}}{\rho(x)} \frac{\partial p}{d x} \\ E &=v_{7} \frac{d}{d x} \ln \left[N_{A}(x)\right] \\ E &=V_{T}\left[\frac{\ln \left(10^{16}\right)-\ln \left(10^{14}\right)}{(2-1) \times 10^{-4}}\right] \\ &=0.026\left[\frac{36-32.23}{1 \times 10^{-4}}\right] \\ &=1198.6 \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{cm} \\ &=1.198 \mathrm{kV} / \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A small percentage of impurity is added to an intrinsic semiconductor at 300 K. Which one of the following statements is true for the energy band diagram shown in the following figure?
options: Intrinsic semiconductor doped with pentavalent atoms to form n-type semiconductor
Intrinsic semiconductor doped with trivalent atoms to form n-type semiconductor
Intrinsic semiconductor doped with pentavalent atoms to form p-type semiconductor
Intrinsic semiconductor doped with trivalent atoms to form p-type semiconductor

questions.text: The energy band diagram and the electron density profile n(x) in a semiconductor are shown in the figures. Assume that [latex]n(x)=10^{15}e^{(\frac{qax}{kT})}cm^{-3}[/latex], with [latex]\alpha[/latex] = 0.1 V/cm and x expressed in cm. Given [latex]\frac{kT}{q}[/latex] = 0.026V, [latex]D_{n}=36 cm^{2}s^{-1}, and \frac{D}{\mu}=\frac{kT}{q}[/latex]. The electron current density (in A/[latex]cm^{2}[/latex] ) at x = 0 is
questions.solution:
The concentration of doping is not uniform throughout the semiconductor, thus to maintain equilibrium internal electric field is generated due to which the band of the semiconductor is varying with slope-0.1 eV/cm.
The generated electric field opposes the diffusion of carriers due to concentration gradient and thus there will be no current flow inside the semiconductor.

questions.text: A dc voltage of 10 V is applied across an n-type silicon bar having a rectangular cross-section and a length of 1 cm as shown in figure. The donor doping concentration [latex]N_{D}[/latex] and the mobility of electrons [latex]\mu_{n}[/latex] are [latex]10^{16} cm^{-3}[/latex] and [latex]1000 cm^{2}V^{-1}s^{-1}[/latex], respectively. The average time (in [latex]\mu s[/latex]) taken by the electrons to move from one end of the bar to other end is ________.
questions.solution:
Electric field inside semiconductor bar,
[latex] E=10 \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{cm}[/latex]
Velocity of electron, [latex]V=\mu E=1 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{cm} / \mathrm{sec} [/latex]
The average time (in [latex]\mu \mathrm{s} [/latex]) taken by the electrons to move from one end of the bar to other end is
[latex] \frac{L}{V}=100 \mu \mathrm{sec}[/latex]

questions.text: A piece of silicon is doped uniformly with phosphorous with a doping concentration of [latex]10^{16}/cm^{3}[/latex]. The expected value of mobility versus doping concentration for silicon assuming full dopant ionization is shown below. The charge of an electron is [latex]1.6 \times 10^{-19}[/latex]C. The conductivity( in S [latex]cm^{-1}[/latex]) of the silicon sample at 300 K is _______.
questions.solution:
As per the graph, mobility of electrons at the concentration [latex]10^{16}/cm^{3} \text{ is } 1200 cm^{2}/V-s. [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { So, } \mu_{n} &=1200 \mathrm{cm}^{2} / \mathrm{V}-\mathrm{s} \\ \sigma_{N} &=N_{D} \mathrm{q} \mu_{n} \\ &=10^{16} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1200=1.92 \mathrm{Scm}^{-1} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: An n-type silicon sample is uniformly illuminated with light which generates [latex]10^{20}[/latex] electron-hole pairs per [latex]cm^{3}[/latex] per second. The minority carrier lifetime in the sample is 1 [latex]\mu s[/latex]. In the steady state, the hole concentration in the sample is approximately [latex]10^{x}[/latex] , where x is an integer. The value of x is ___.
questions.solution:
The concentration of hole-electron par in
[latex] 1 \mu \mathrm{sec}=10^{20} \times 10^{-6}=10^{14} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}[/latex]
So, the power of 10 is 14
[latex] x=14[/latex]

questions.text: A silicon sample is uniformly doped with donor type impurities with a concentration of [latex]10^{16} /cm^{3}[/latex]. The electron and hole mobilities in the sample are 1200 [latex]cm^{2}/V-s [/latex] and 400 [latex]cm^{2}[/latex]/V-s respectively. Assume complete ionization of impurities. The charge of an electron is [latex]1.6  \times 10^{-19}[/latex] C. The resistivity of the sample (in [latex]\Omega[/latex]-cm) is ____________.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{\sigma_{N}}=\frac{1}{N_{D} q \mu_{n}} \\ &=\frac{1}{10^{16} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1200}=0.52 \Omega-\mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
An N -type semiconductor having uniform doping is biased as shown in the figure.

If [latex]E_{C}[/latex] is the lowest energy level of the conduction band, [latex]E_{V}[/latex] is the highest energy level of the valance band and [latex]E_{F}[/latex] is the Fermi level, which one of the following represents the energy band diagram for the biased N -type semiconductor ?

Consider a silicon sample doped with [latex]N_{D}=1\times10^{15}/cm^{3}[/latex]  donor atoms. Assume that the intrinsic carrier concentration [latex]n_{i}=1.5\times10^{10}/cm^{3}[/latex]. If the sample is additionally doped with [latex]N_{A}=1\times10^{18}/cm^{3}[/latex] acceptor atoms, the approximate number of electrons/[latex]cm^{3}[/latex]  in the sample, at T = 300 K, will be _____.
questions.solution:
For a compensated p-type semiconductor, the minority carrier electron concentration is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} n_{0} &=\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{\left(N_{A}-N_{D}\right)} \\ n_{0} &=\frac{2.25 \times 10^{20}}{\left(10^{18}-10^{15}\right)}=225.2 \mathrm{cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The cut-off wavelength (in [latex]\mu[/latex] m) of light that can be used for intrinsic excitation of a semiconductor material of bandgap [latex]E_{g}[/latex] = 1.1 eV is _____.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \quad \lambda_{c}&=\frac{1.24}{E_{g}(\mathrm{eV})} \mu \mathrm{m}=\frac{1.24}{1.1} \mu \mathrm{m} \\ \lambda_{c}&=1.12 \mu \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: In the figure, [latex] ln(\rho _{i}[/latex]) is plotted as a function of 1/T , where [latex]\rho _{i}[/latex] is the intrinsic resistivity of silicon, T is the temperature, and the plot is almost linear. The slope of the line can be used to estimate
options: sum of electron and hole mobility in silicon [latex](\mu _{n}+\mu _{p})[/latex]
reciprocal of the sum of electron and hole mobility in silicon [latex](\mu _{n}+\mu _{p})^{-1}[/latex]

questions.text: At  T = 300 K, the band gap and the intrinsic carrier concentration of GaAs are 1.42 eV and [latex]10^{6}cm^{-3}[/latex], respectively. In order to generate electron hole pairs in GaAs, which one of the wavelength [latex](\lambda _{C})[/latex] ranges of incident radiation, is most suitable ? (Given that : Plank's constant is [latex]6.62 \times 10^{-34}[/latex]J-s, velocity of light is [latex]3 \times 10^{10} cm/s[/latex] and charge of electron is [latex]1.6*10^{-19}[/latex]C)
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \lambda_{c} \leq \frac{1.24}{E_{g}(e V)} \mu \mathrm{m} \\ \lambda_{c} \leq \frac{1.24}{1.42} \\ \lambda_{c} \leq 0.87 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{array}[/latex]

questions.text: At T = 300 K, the hole mobility of a semiconductor [latex]\mu _{P}=500 cm^{2}/V-s [/latex] and [latex] \frac{KT}{q}=26mV[/latex]. The hole diffusion constant [latex]D_{P} \; in \; cm^{2}/s[/latex]  is _____.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \frac{D_{p}}{\mu_{p}}=v_{T} \\ D_{p}=\mu_{p} V_{T}=500 \times 26 \times 10^{-3} \\ D_{p}=13 \mathrm{cm}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \end{array}[/latex]

questions.text: A thin P-type silicon sample is uniformly illuminated with light which generates excess carriers. The recombination rate is directly proportional to

When a silicon diode having a doping concentration of [latex]N_{A}=9\times10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] on p -side and [latex]N_{D}=1\times10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] on n-side is reverse biased, the total depletion width is found to be 3 [latex]\mu[/latex] m. Given that the permittivity of silicon is [latex]1.04\times10^{-12}[/latex] F/cm, the depletion width on the p-side and the maximum electric field in the depletion region, respectively, are
questions.solution:
We know that
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{N_{A}}{N_{D}}&=\frac{x_{n}}{x_{p}}\\ So, \frac{N_{A}}{N_{D}}+1&=\frac{x_{n}}{x_{p}}+1 \\ \frac{N_{A}+N_{D}}{N_{D}}&=\frac{x_{n}+x_{p}}{x_{p}}\\ \frac{10^{17}}{10^{16}} &=\frac{3 \mu m}{x_{p}} \\ \therefore \quad x_{p} &=0.3 \mu \mathrm{m}\\ \text{and}\\ E_{\max }&=\frac{q N_{A} x_{p}}{\epsilon_{s}}=\frac{q N_{D} x_{n}}{\epsilon_{s}} \\ \therefore E_{\max } &=\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 9 \times 10^{16} \times 0.3 \times 10^{-4}}{1.04 \times 10^{-12}} \\ E_{\max } &=4.15 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: Assume electronic charge [latex]q=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C[/latex], kT/q=25mV and electron mobility [latex]\mu _{n}=1000cm^{2} /V-s [/latex] . If the concentration gradient of electrons injected into a P-type silicon sample is [latex]1 \times 10^{21}/cm^{4}[/latex], the magnitude of electron diffusion current density (in [latex]A/cm^{2}[/latex]) is _____.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} J &=q D_{n} \frac{d n}{d x} \\ \text { where, } D_{n} &=\mu_{n} V_{T} \\ D_{n} &=\frac{1000 \mathrm{cm}^{2}}{V s} \times 25 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{V} \\ D_{n} &=25 \mathrm{cm}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ \text { then, } \quad J &=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 25 \times 1 \times 10^{21} \\ J &=4000 \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A silicon bar is doped with donor impurities [latex]N_{D}=2.25\times10^{15} atom/cm^{3}[/latex]. Given the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon at T = 300 K is [latex]n_{i}=1.5\times10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex]. Assuming complete impurity ionization, the equilibrium election and hole concentrations are
questions.solution:
since [latex]N_{D} \gt \gt n_{i}[/latex]
therefore equilibrium electron concentration is
[latex] n \simeq N_{D}=2.25 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{cm}^{-3}[/latex]
And equilibrium hole concentration is given by mass action law
[latex] p=\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{N_{D}}=\frac{\left(1.5 \times 10^{10}\right)^{2}}{2.25 \times 10^{15}}=1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{cm}^{-3}[/latex]

questions.text: The doping concentrations on the p-side and n-side of a silicon diode are [latex]1\times 10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] and [latex]1 \times 10^{17}cm^{-3}[/latex], respectively. A forward bias of 0.3 V is applied to the diode. At T=300K, the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon [latex]n_{i}=1.5 \times 10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] and [latex]\frac{KT}{q}=26mV[/latex]. The electron concentration at the edge of the depletion region on the p-side is
questions.solution:
The electron concentration at the edge of the depletion region on the p-side is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} n_{p} &=n_{p_{0}} \exp \left[\frac{q V_{t}}{k T}\right] \\ \text { where, } n_{p_{0}} &=\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{N_{A}} \\ n_{p_{0}} &=\frac{\left(1.5 \times 10^{10}\right)^{2}}{10^{16}}=2.25 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
We then have
[latex] \begin{array}{l} n_{p}=2.25 \times 10^{4} \exp \left[\frac{0.3}{0.026}\right]\\ n_{p}=2.25 \times 10^{4} \times 1.025 \times 10^{5} \\ n_{0}=2.306 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{cm}^{-3} \end{array}[/latex]

questions.text:
An ideal p-n junction germanium diode has a reverse saturation current of [latex]10 \mu \mathrm{~A}[/latex] at 300 K .

The voltage (in Volts, rounded off to two decimal places) to be applied across the junction to get a forward bias current of 100 mA at 300 K is __________ .

(Consider the Boltzmann constant [latex]\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{K}[/latex] and the charge of an electron [latex]\mathrm{e}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}[/latex].)
questions.solution:
[latex] I = I_s \left( e^{\frac{eV}{k_BT}} - 1 \right) [/latex]
Where: [latex] I = 100\ \text{mA} = 0.1\ \text{A} [/latex]
[latex] I_s = 10\ \mu\text{A} = 10 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{A} [/latex]
[latex] T = 300\ \text{K} [/latex]
[latex] e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C} [/latex]
[latex] k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J/K} [/latex]

Approximate since [latex] I \gg I_s [/latex], so: [latex] I \approx I_s e^{\frac{eV}{k_BT}} [/latex]
Taking natural logarithm on both sides: [latex] \frac{eV}{k_BT} = \ln\left(\frac{I}{I_s}\right) [/latex]
[latex] V = \frac{k_BT}{e} \ln\left(\frac{I}{I_s}\right) [/latex]

Now plug in the values: [latex] \frac{k_BT}{e} = \frac{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.025875\ \text{V} [/latex]
[latex] \ln\left(\frac{0.1}{10 \times 10^{-6}}\right) = \ln(10000) = \ln(10^4) = 4 \ln(10) \approx 4 \times 2.3026 = 9.2104 [/latex]

So, [latex] V = 0.025875 \times 9.2104 \approx 0.2382\ \text{V} [/latex]

questions.text: A p-type semiconductor with zero electric field is under illumination (low level injection) in steady state condition. Excess minority carrier density is zero at [latex] x=\pm 2l_n[/latex], where [latex] l_n=10^{-4} cm[/latex] is the diffusion length of electrons. Assume electronic charge, [latex] q=-1.6 \times 10^{-19}C[/latex]. The profiles of photo-generation rate of carriers and the recombination rate of excess minority carriers (R) are shown. Under these conditions, the magnitude of the current density due to the photo-generated electrons at [latex] x=+2l_n[/latex] is _________ [latex] mA/cm^2[/latex] (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.solution:
Given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta _n(x)&=R\tau _n=10^{20}e^{-|x|/l_n}\cdot \tau _n\\ \delta (l_n)&=10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n \;\;\;...(i)\\ for \;\; l_n\leq x\leq 2l_n \end{aligned}[/latex]
Continuity equation is given by
[latex] D_n\frac{\partial^2 \delta _n}{\partial x^2}+G-R \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
G and R both are zero - for [latex] [l_n\leq x\leq 2l_n][/latex]
Hence Equation (i) reduced to [latex] D_n \frac{\partial^n \delta _n }{\partial x^2}=0[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \delta _n(x)=Ax+B[/latex]
For calculating A and B we use Boundary condition
[latex] \delta _n(2l_n)=0\; \Rightarrow A=\frac{-B}{2l_n}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \delta _n(x)=\frac{-B}{2l_n}x+B=B\left [ 1-\frac{x}{2l_n} \right ] \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
At [latex]x=l_n [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} 10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n&=B\left [ 1-\frac{l_n}{2l_n} \right ] \\ B&= 2 \times 10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n\\ \therefore \; \delta _n(x) &=2 \times 10^{20} e^{-1}\tau _n\left [ 1-\frac{x}{2l_n} \right ] \end{aligned} [/latex]
for [latex]l_n \leq x \leq 2l_n [/latex]
Electron diffusion current density is given by [latex] |J_n|_{diff}=qD_n\frac{d\eta }{dx}=qD_n \times 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1} \times \tau _n\left [ 0-\frac{1}{2l_n} \right ][/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times l_n ^2 \times 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1}}{2l_n}[/latex]
[latex]=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times l_n \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1} [/latex]
[latex] =1.6 \times 10 \times 1 \times 10^{-4} \times e^{-1}[/latex]
[latex] =0.59mA/cm^2[/latex]

questions.text:
A silicon P-N junction is shown in the figure. The doping in the P region is [latex]5\times10^{16}\:cm^{-3}[/latex] and doping in the N region is [latex]10\times10^{16}\:cm^{-3}[/latex]. The parameters given are
Built-in voltage [latex]\left ( \Phi _{\text{bi}} \right ) = 0.8\:V[/latex]
Electron charge [latex](q) = 1.6\times10^{-19} C\:[/latex]
Vacuum permittivity [latex]\left ( \varepsilon _{0} \right ) = 8.85\times10^{-12}\:F/m[/latex]
Relative permittivity of silicon [latex]\left ( \varepsilon _{\text{Si}} \right ) = 12[/latex]

he magnitude of reverse bias voltage that would completely deplete one of the two regions (P or N) prior to the other (rounded off to one decimal place) is _________V.
questions.solution:
Given: [latex]\quad N_{A}=5 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \quad ; \quad N_{D}=10 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]
Built-in potential, [latex]\quad \phi_{\mathrm{bi}}=0.8 \mathrm{~V} [/latex]
Electron charge, [latex]q=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
Vacuum permittivity, [latex]\epsilon_{o}=8.85 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~F} / \mathrm{m}=8.85 \times 10^{-14} \mathrm{~F} / \mathrm{cm}[/latex]
Relative permittivity silicon,
[latex] \epsilon_{\mathrm{si}}=12[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow [/latex] Doping on both sides is comparable, so smaller region would deplete first.
So, depletion region width on N -side [latex]=x_{n}=0.2 \mu \mathrm{m}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \qquad x_{n}&=0.2 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm}\\ x_{n}&=\sqrt{\frac{2 \epsilon_{S i}}{q}\left(\frac{N_{A}}{N_{D}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{N_{A}+N_{D}}\right)\left(\phi_{b i}+V_{R}\right)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
where, [latex]V_{R} \rightarrow [/latex] Magnitude of reverse bias potential
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad 0.2 \times 10^{-4}&=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 12 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \cdot \frac{5 \times 10^{16}}{10 \times 10^{16}} \cdot \frac{1}{\left(15 \times 10^{16}\right)}\left(\phi_{b i}+V_{R}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad \phi_{b j}+V_{R}&=9.039\\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad V_{R}&=9.039-0.8\\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad V_{R}&=8.239 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A pn junction solar cell of area 1.0 [latex]cm^{2}[/latex], illuminated uniformly with 100 mW [latex]cm^{-2}[/latex], has the following parameters: Efficiency = 15%, open circuit voltage = 0.7 V, fill factor = 0.8, and thickness = 200 [latex]\mu m[/latex], The charge of an electron is [latex]1.6 \times 10^{-19}[/latex]C. questions.text: A one-sided abrupt [latex]pn[/latex] junction diode has a depletion capacitance CD of 50 pF at a reverse bias of 0.2 V. The plot of [latex]1/C_D^2[/latex] versus the applied voltage V for this diode is a straight line as shown in the figure below. The slope of the plot is ____[latex]\times 10^{20} F^{-2} V^{-1}[/latex].
questions.solution:
As per GATE official answer key MTA (Marks to ALL)

Depletion or transition capacitance is,
[latex]C_{D}=\frac{A_{\epsilon }}{W}[/latex]
For one-sided PN junction [latex]\left (EX:P^{+}N Junction \right )[/latex]
[latex]W=\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon V_{B}}{eN_{D}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon \left ( V_{bi}-V \right )}{eN_{D}}}[/latex]
where V is anode to cathode applied potential.
[latex]\Rightarrow \, \, \, \, C_{D}=\frac{A\epsilon }{\sqrt{\frac{2\, \epsilon \left ( V_{bi}-V \right )}{eN_{D}}}} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \, \, \, \, \frac{1}{C_{D}^{2}}=\frac{2}{A^{2}\epsilon eN_{D}}\left ( V_{bi}-V \right )[/latex]
[latex] \frac{1}{C_{D}^{2}}\, becomes \, zero \, at V=V_{bi}[/latex]
From above graph,[latex]y=\frac{1}{C_{D}^{2}}=0\, at\, x_{1}=V_{bi}[/latex]
[latex] And \, \, \, y_{2}=\frac{1}{C_{D}^{2}}=4\times 10^{20}\, at\, x_{2}=-0.2V [/latex]
[latex]Slope=\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-X_{1}}=\frac{4\times 10^{20}-0}{-0.2-V_{bi}}[/latex]
[latex] V_{bi}[/latex] is not provided,slope cannot be found.

questions.text: A Germanium sample of dimensions 1cmx1cm is illuminated with a 20 mW, 600 nm laser light source as shown in the figure. [latex]\begin{aligned} P_{\text {absorbed }} &=P_{\text {incident }}\left(1-e^{-\alpha T}\right) \\ \frac{1}{3} &=\frac{2}{3}\left(1-e^{-\alpha T}\right) \\ \frac{2}{3} e^{-\alpha T} &=\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad T &=\frac{1}{\alpha} \ln (2)=\frac{1}{3 \times 10^{4}} \ln (2) \mathrm{cm} \\ &=0.231 \mu \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The quantum efficiency ([latex]\eta[/latex]) and responsivity (R) at a wavelength [latex]\lambda (in \; \mu m)[/latex] in a p-i-n photodetector are related by
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \eta&=\frac{I_{\text {out }}}{q} \times \frac{h f}{P_{\text {in }}} \\ R&=\frac{I_{\text {out }}}{P_{\text {in }}}\\ \text{So, }\quad R&=\eta \times \frac{q}{h f}=\eta \times \frac{q \lambda}{h c} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
If [latex]\lambda[/latex] is given in [latex]\mu \mathrm{m},[/latex] then
[latex] \begin{aligned} R &=\eta \lambda \times \frac{q \times 10^{-6}}{h c} \\ \frac{h c}{q \times 10^{-6}} & \simeq 1.24\\ \text{So, }\quad R&=\frac{\eta \lambda}{1.24} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: Which one of the following options describes correctly the equilibrium band diagram at T=300 K of a Silicon [latex]pnp^+p^{++}[/latex] configuration shown in the figure?

A junction is made between [latex] p^{-} Si [/latex] with doping density [latex] N_{A1} = 10^{15} cm^{-3}[/latex] and pSi with doping density[latex] N_{A2} = 10^{17} cm^{-3} [/latex].
Given: Boltzmann constant [latex]k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} JK^{-1} [/latex], electronic charge [latex] q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} C [/latex]. Assume 100% acceptor ionization.
At room temperature (T = 300K), the magnitude of the built-in potential (in volts, correct to two decimal places) across this junction will be _________________.
questions.solution:
Built-in potential,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{b i} &=\frac{k T}{q} \ln \left(\frac{N_{A 2}}{N_{A 1}}\right) \\ &=\frac{1.38 \times 3}{1.6 \times 100} \ln (100) \mathrm{V}=0.1192 \mathrm{V} \\ & \simeq 0.12 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A solar cell of area  1.0 [latex]cm^{2}[/latex] , operating at 1.0 sun intensity, has a short circuit current of 20 mA, and an open circuit voltage of 0.65 V. Assuming room temperature operation and thermal equivalent voltage of 26mV, the open circuit voltage (in volts, correct to two decimal places) at 0.2 sun intensity is _______.
questions.solution:
For solar cell,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{OC}} &=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{I_{S C}}{I_{O}}\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2}-V_{\mathrm{OC} 1} &=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{I_{S C 2}}{I_{S C}}\right)=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{0.20}{1.0}\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2} &=V_{\mathrm{OC} 1}-0.026 \mathrm{ln}(5) \\ &=0.65-0.041845=0.608 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: Red (R), Green (G) and Blue (B) Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) were fabricated using p-n junctions of three different inorganic semiconductors having different band-gaps. The builtin voltages of red, green and blue diodes are [latex] V_{R}, V_{G} \; and \; V_{B} [/latex], respectively. Assume donor and acceptor doping to be the same [latex] (N_{A} \; and \; N_{D} [/latex], respectively) in the p and n sides of all the three diodes. Which one of the following relationships about the built-in voltages is TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]\lambda_{R} \gt \lambda_{G} \gt \lambda_{B}[/latex]
Energy gap, [latex] E_{g} \propto \frac{1}{\lambda} [/latex]
So, [latex]E_{g R} \lt E_{g G} \lt E_{g B}[/latex]
Materials with high energy gap will have high built-in voltages, when doping concentrations are same.
So, [latex]V_{R} \lt V_{G} \lt V_{B}[/latex]

questions.text: A p-n step junction diode with a contact potential of 0.65V has a depletion width of 1[latex]\mu[/latex]m at equilibrium. The forward voltage (in volts, correct to two decimal places) at which this width reduces to 0.6 [latex]\mu[/latex]m is _______.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} W_{\mathrm{dep}} &=\sqrt{\frac{2 \varepsilon}{q}\left(\frac{1}{N_{A}}+\frac{1}{N_{D}}\right)\left(V_{b i}-V_{A K}\right)} \\ \frac{\sqrt{\left(0.65-V_{A K}\right)}}{\sqrt{0.65}} &=\frac{0.6 \mu \mathrm{m}}{1 \mu \mathrm{m}}=0.6 \\ 1-\frac{V_{A K}}{0.65} &=0.36 \\ V_{A K} &=0.65(1-0.36) \\ &=0.65 \times 0.64=0.416 \mathrm{V} \simeq 0.42 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: For a particular intensity of incident light on a silicon pn junction solar cell, the photocurrent density ([latex]J_{L}[/latex]) is 2.5 mA/[latex]cm^{2}[/latex] and the open-circuit voltage ([latex]V_{oc}[/latex]) is 0.451 V. consider thermal voltage ([latex]V_{T}[/latex]) to be 25mV. If the intensity of the incident light is increased by 20 times,assuming that the temperature remains unchanged. [latex]V_{oc} [/latex](in volts) will be ______.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{OC}} &=V_{T} \ln \frac{J_{L}}{J_{S}} \quad J_{L} \propto \text { Light intensity } \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2}-V_{\mathrm{OC} 1} &=V_{T} \ln \frac{J_{L 2}}{J_{L 1}} \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2}-V_{\mathrm{OC} 1} &=25 \ln 20 \cong 75 \mathrm{mV}=0.075 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2} &=0.451 \mathrm{V}+0.075 \mathrm{V}=0.526 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: An abrupt pn junction (located at x = 0) is uniformly doped on both p and n sides. The width of the depletion region is W and the electric field variation in the x-direction is E(x). Which of the following figures represents the electric field profile near the pn junction?

As shown, two Silicon (Si) abrupt p-n junction diodes are fabricated with uniform donor doping concentration of [latex]N_{D1}=10^{14}cm^{-3}[/latex] and [latex]N_{D2}=10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] in the n-regions of the diodes, and uniform acceptor doping concentration of [latex]N_{A1}=10^{14}cm^{-3} [/latex] and [latex]N_{A2}=10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] in the pregions of the diodes, respectively. Assuming that the reverse bias voltage is [latex]\gt \gt[/latex] built-in potentials of the diodes, the ratio [latex]\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}}[/latex] of their reverse bias capacitances for the same applied reverse bias, is __________.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} W&=\sqrt{\frac{2 \varepsilon V_{R}}{e}\left(\frac{1}{N_{A}}+\frac{1}{N_{D}}\right)} \\ \because \; &V_{R}\gt \gt V_{bi}\\ \text{Under reverse } &\text{biased condition,}\\ C&=\frac{\varepsilon A}{W} \quad \Rightarrow C \propto \frac{1}{W}\\ \text{So}\quad\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}} &=\frac{W_{1}}{W_{2}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{2 \varepsilon V_{R}}{e}\left(\frac{2}{10^{14}}\right)}{\frac{2 \varepsilon V_{R}}{e}\left(\frac{2}{10^{16}}\right)}}=10 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: An [latex]n^{+} -n[/latex] Silicon device is fabricated with uniform and non-degenerate donor doping concentrations of [latex]N_{D1}=1 \times 10^{18}cm^{-3}[/latex]  and [latex]N_{D2}=1 \times 10^{15}cm^{-3}[/latex] corresponding to the [latex]n^{+}[/latex] and n regions respectively. At the operational temperature T, assume complete impurity ionization, kT/q = 25 mV, and intrinsic carrier concentration to be [latex]n_{i}=1 \times 10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex] . What is the magnitude of the built-in potential of this device?
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{0} &=V_{T} \ln \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}=V_{T} \ln \frac{N_{D 1}}{N_{D 2}} \\ &=0.25 \ln \frac{10^{18}}{10^{15}}=0.025 \ln (1000) \\ &=0.173 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The figure shows the I-V characteristics of a solar cell illuminated uniformly with solar light of power [latex]100 mW/cm^{2}[/latex]. The solar cell has an area of [latex]3cm^{2}[/latex] and a fill factor of 0.7. The maximum efficiency (in %) of the device is __________
questions.solution:
Fill factor [latex]=\frac{\text { Maximum obtained power }}{V_{O C} \cdot I_{S C}} [/latex]

Efficiency [latex]\eta=\frac{P_{m}}{G \cdot A}=\frac{0.063}{100 \times 10^{-3} \times 3}=21 \% [/latex]
G [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] input light in [latex]\mathrm{W} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider a region of silicon devoid of electrons and holes, with an ionized donor density of [latex]N_{d}^{+}=10^{17}cm^{-3}[/latex]. The electric field at x= 0 is 0 V/cm and the electric field at x=L is 50 kV/cm in the positive x direction. Assume that the electric field is zero in the y and z directions at all points.

Given [latex]q=1.6\times 10^{-19}[/latex]coulomb, [latex]\epsilon _{0}=8.85\times 10^{-14}F/cm,\epsilon _{r}=11.7[/latex] for silicon, the value of L in nm is ________
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} |\varepsilon|&=\frac{q}{\varepsilon} N_{D} X_{N} \\ 50 \times 10^{3}&=\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{8.85 \times 10^{-14} \times 11.7} \times 10^{17} \times X_{N} \\ \text { On solving, } \quad X_{N} &=3.2356 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{cm} \\ &=3.236 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{m} \\ x_{N} &=L=32.36 \mathrm{nm}\\ &=L=32.36 \mathrm{nm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: Consider avalanche breakdown in a silicon [latex]p^{+}n[/latex] junction. The n-region is uniformly doped with a donor density [latex]N_{D}[/latex]. Assume that breakdown occurs when the magnitude of the electric field at any point in the device becomes equal to the critical field [latex]E_{crit}[/latex]. Assume [latex]E_{crit}[/latex] to be independent of [latex]N_{D}[/latex]. If the built-in voltage of the [latex]p^{+}n[/latex] junction is much smaller than the breakdown voltage,[latex]V_{BR}[/latex], the relationship between [latex]V_{BR}[/latex] and [latex]N_{D}[/latex] is given by
questions.solution:
In any type of PN junction
[latex] \begin{aligned} v_{B R} &\propto \frac{1}{\text { Doping Concentration }}\\ \text{i.e.}\quad V_{B R} &\propto \frac{1}{N_{D}} \text { (or) } V_{B R}=\frac{\varepsilon E^{2}}{2 q N_{D}} \\ \therefore V_{BR} \times N_{D} \rightarrow &\text { is a constant } \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider a silicon p-n junction with a uniform acceptor doping concentration of [latex]10^{17}cm^{-3}[/latex] on the pside and a uniform donor doping concentration of [latex]10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] on the n-side. No external voltage is applied to the diode. Given: kT/q=26mV, [latex]n_{i}=1.5\times 10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex], [latex]\varepsilon _{Si}=12\varepsilon _{0},\varepsilon _{0}=8.85\times 10^{-14}F/m,[/latex] and [latex]q=1.6\times 10^{-19}C[/latex].
The charge per unit junction area (nC [latex]cm^{-2}[/latex]) in the depletion region on the p-side is ___________
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{0}&=V_{T} \ln \frac{N_{A} N_{D}}{n_{i}^{2}} \\ &=26 \times 10^{-3} \ln \frac{10^{16} \times 10^{17}}{\left(1.5 \times 10^{10}\right)^{2}} \\ V_{0}&=0.757 \mathrm{V} \\ W&=\sqrt{\frac{2 \varepsilon}{q}\left(\frac{1}{N_{A}}+\frac{1}{N_{D}}\right) V_{0}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-16} \times 12}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}\left[\frac{1}{10^{16}}+\frac{1}{10^{17}}\right] 0.757} \\ W&=3.3255 \mu \mathrm{cm} \\ W_{P}&=\frac{W N_{D}}{N_{A}+N_{D}}=\frac{3.3255 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{16}}{10^{16}+10^{17}} \\ &=0.3023 \mu \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Charge per unit junction area in the depletion layer
on p side is
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=-q N_{A} W_{P} \\ &=-1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{17} \times 0.3023 \times 10^{-6} \\ &=-4.8368 \mathrm{nC} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The electric field profile in the depletion region of a p-n junction in equilibrium is shown in the figure. Which one of the following statements is NOT TRUE?
options: The left side of the junction is n-type and the right side is p-type

If the p-type region has a doping concentration of [latex]10^{15} cm^{-3}[/latex], then the doping concentration in the n-type region will be [latex]10^{16} cm^{-3}[/latex]
questions.solution:
Built in potential,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Psi_{0} &=\frac{1}{2} \times\left(10^{6} \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{m}\right) \times\left(1.1 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}\right) \\ &=0.55 \mathrm{Volts} \end{aligned}[/latex]
But in question (option (c)) is given as 700 mV.

questions.text: For a silicon diode with long P and N regions, the accepter and donor impurity concentrations are [latex]1 \times 10^{17} cm^{-3}[/latex] and [latex] 1 \times 10^{15} cm^{-3}[/latex], respectively. The lifetimes of electrons in P region and holes in N region are both 100 [latex]\mu s[/latex]. The electron and hole diffusion coefficients are [latex]49 cm^{2}/s \; and \; 36 cm^{2}/s[/latex], respectively. Assume kT/q = 26 mV, the intrinsic carrier concentration is [latex]1 \times 10^{10} cm^{-3}, \; and \;  q = 1.6 \times  10^{-19}[/latex] C. When a forward voltage of 208 mV is applied across the diode, the hole current density (in nA/[latex]cm^{2}[/latex]) injected from P region to N region is _____________.
questions.solution:
The hole current density injected from P region to N region is given by
[latex] \frac{q n_{i}^{2} D_{p}}{N_{D} L_{p}}\left[\exp \left(\frac{V_{F B}}{\eta V_{T}}\right)-1\right][/latex]
where,
q= charge on electron
[latex] n_{i}=[/latex] Intrinsic carrier concentration in silicon
[latex] N_{D}=[/latex] Donor doping
[latex] D_{p}=[/latex] Hole diffusion coefficient
[latex] L_{p}=[/latex] Mean diffusion length of hole
[latex] V_{F B}=[/latex] Forward voltage applied across diode
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{T}=& k T / q=26 \mathrm{mV} \\ L_{p} &=\sqrt{\tau_{p} D_{p}}=\sqrt{100 \times 10^{-6} \times 36} \\ &=0.06 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using the above values, we get hole current density injected from P region to N region

questions.text: The built-in potential of an abrupt p-n junction is 0.75 V. If its junction capacitance [latex](C_{J})[/latex] at a reverse bias [latex](V_{R})[/latex] of 1.25 V is 5 pF, the value of [latex]C_{J}[/latex] (in pF) when [latex]V_{R}[/latex] = 7.25 V is ________.
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} C_{j} &\propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{V_{b i}+V_{R}}} \\ \frac{C_{2 j}}{C_{1 j}}&=\sqrt{\frac{V_{b i}+V_{R_{1}}}{V_{b i}+V_{R_{2}}}} \\ C_{2 j}&=C_{1 j} \sqrt{\frac{2}{8}}=\frac{C_{1 j}}{2}=2.5 \mathrm{pF} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, answer is 2.5

questions.text: The donor and accepter impurities in an abrupt junction silicon diode are [latex]1 \times 10^{16} cm^{-3} [/latex] and [latex] 5 \times 10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex], respectively. Assume that the intrinsic carrier concentration in silicon [latex]n_{i}=1.5 \times 10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex] at  300K, [latex]\frac{kT}{q}=26mV[/latex] and the permittivity of silicon [latex]\varepsilon_{st} =1.04 \times 12^{-12}F/cm[/latex]. The built-in potential and the depletion width of the diode under thermal equilibrium conditions, respectively, are
questions.solution:
Built-in potential is given by,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{b i}&=V_{T} \ln \left[\frac{N_{A} N_{D}}{n_{i}^{2}}\right] \\ V_{b i}&=0.026 \ln \left[\frac{10^{16} \times 5 \times 10^{18}}{2.25 \times 10^{20}}\right] \\ V_{b i}&=0.86 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]
and depletion width W is given by,
[latex] \begin{aligned} W&=\sqrt{\frac{2 \epsilon}{q}\left[\frac{1}{N_{A}}+\frac{1}{N_{D}}\right] V_{b i}}\\ W&=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.04 \times 10^{-12}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}\left[\frac{1}{5 \times 10^{18}}+\frac{1}{10^{16}}\right] \times 0.86} \\ W&=3.3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: Consider an abrupt PN junction (at T = 300 K) shown in the figure. The depletion region width [latex]X_{n}[/latex] on the N -side of the junction is 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex] m and the permittivity of silicon ([latex]\varepsilon_{st}[/latex]) is [latex]1.044\times 10^{-12}[/latex] F/cm. At the junction, the approximate value of the peak electric field (in kV/cm) is_____.
questions.solution:
For abrupt [latex]P^{+}[/latex] N junction
[latex] E_{\max }[/latex] is given:
[latex] \begin{aligned} E_{\max } &=\frac{-q N_{0} x_{n}}{\epsilon_{s}}\qquad\left[\begin{array}{c} \because N_{A}>>N_{D} \\ W \simeq x_{n} \end{array}\right] \\ \Rightarrow E_{\max }&=\frac{-1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{16} \times 0.2 \times 10^{-4}}{1.044 \times 10^{-12}} \\ E_{\max } &=-30.65 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{cm} \\ E_{\max } &=-30.65 \mathrm{kV} / \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: When the optical power incident on a photodiode is 10[latex]\mu[/latex]W and the responsivity is 0.8 A/W, the photocurrent generated (in [latex]\mu[/latex]  A) is _____.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \text { Responsivity }(R)=\frac{I_{p}}{P_{o}} \\ \text { where } I_{p}=\text { Photo current } \\ \qquad P_{0}=\text { Incident power } \\ \therefore \quad I_{p}=R \times P_{0}=8 \mu \mathrm{A} \end{array}[/latex]

questions.text: In a forward biased pn junction diode, the sequence of events that best describes the mechanism of current flow is
options: injection, and subsequent diffusion and recombination of minority carriers
injection, and subsequent drift and generation of minority carriers
extraction, and subsequent diffusion and generation of minority carriers
extraction, and subsequent drift and recombination of minority carriers
questions.solution: In a forward biased pn-junction diode, the current  flow is due to diffusion of majority carriers and  recombination of minority carriers.

questions.text:
The i-v characteristics of the diode in the circuit given below are [latex]i=\left\{\begin{matrix} \frac{v-0.7}{500}A &v\geq 0.7V \\ 0 A & v \lt 0.7 V \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]

The current in the circuit is
questions.solution:
Applying KVL in given circuit we have
[latex] 10-1000 i-v=0 \qquad\ldots(1)[/latex]
since 10 V is greater than 0.7 V so current will flow through diode and is
[latex] i=\frac{v-0.7}{500}\qquad\ldots(2)[/latex]
from (1) and (2) we have,
[latex] \begin{aligned} 10-2(v-0.7)-v &=0 \\ 10+1.4-3 v &=0 \\ 3 v &=11.4 \\ v &=\frac{11.4}{3}=3.8 v\\ \text{so}\quad i &=\frac{v-0.7}{500}=\frac{3.8-0.7}{500} \\ &=6.2 \mathrm{mA} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider a silicon p-n junction at room temperature having the following parameters:

questions.solution:

At the centre x=0

questions.text: At 300 K, for a diode current of 1 mA, a certain germanium diode requires a forward bias of 0.1435 V, whereas a certain silicon diode requires a forward bias of 0.718 V. Under the conditions state above, the closest approximation of the ratio of reverse saturation current in germanium diode to that in silicon diode is
questions.solution:
[latex]\eta=1 [/latex] for Germanium
[latex] \eta=2 [/latex] for Silicon at low value of current
[latex] \begin{aligned} I&=I_{O S i}\left(e^{\frac{V_{D 1}}{\eta V_{T}}}-1\right) &\ldots(i)\\ I&=I_{O G e}\left(e^{\frac{V_{D 2}}{\eta V_{T}}}-1\right)&\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
L.H.S. of (i) = (ii)
[latex] \Rightarrow I_{O_{S i}}\left(e^{\frac{V_{D 1}}{\eta V_{T}}}-1\right)=I_{O_{G e}}\left(e^{\frac{V_{D 2}}{\eta V_{T}}}-1\right) [/latex]
[latex] \frac{I_{O_{Ge}}}{I_{O_{Si}}}=\frac{e^{\frac{V_{D_{1}}}{\eta V_{T}}}-1}{e^{\frac{V_{D_{2}}}{\eta V_{T}}}-1}=\frac{e^{\frac{0.718}{2 \times 26 \times 10^{-3}}}-1}{e^{\frac{0.1435}{26 \times 10^{-3}}}-1}=4 \times 10^{3}[/latex]

questions.text:
An n-channel MOSFET is connected as shown in the Figure.

Assume [latex]V_{TH} = 1 \text{ V}[/latex], [latex]V_{DD} = 5 \text{ V}[/latex], and [latex]\mu C_{ox} (W/L) = 2 \text{ mA V}^{-2}[/latex] and neglect channel length modulation effects.

The gate voltage ([latex]V_G[/latex]) of the n-channel MOSFET (in Volt) is ____. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.solution:
Given:
Diode-connected n-channel MOSFET (gate tied to drain), [latex]V_{DD}=5\text{ V}[/latex], [latex]R_D=1\text{ k}\Omega[/latex] from [latex]V_{DD}[/latex] to drain, [latex]V_{TH}=1\text{ V}[/latex], [latex]\mu C_{ox}(W/L)=2\text{ mA/V}^2[/latex].

Step 1: Since gate = drain, [latex]V_{GS}=V_{DS}=V_G[/latex] (source at ground)

MOSFET is in saturation ([latex]V_{DS}\geq V_{GS}-V_{TH}[/latex] always satisfied for diode-connected).

Step 2: KVL

[latex] V_{DD} = I_D \cdot R_D + V_G [/latex]
[latex] I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times2\times(V_G-1)^2 = (V_G-1)^2\text{ mA} [/latex]

Step 3: Substitute

[latex] 5 = (V_G-1)^2 \times 1\text{k} \times 10^{-3} + V_G [/latex] [latex] 5 = (V_G-1)^2 + V_G [/latex]
Let [latex]u = V_G - 1[/latex]:
[latex] 5 = u^2 + u + 1 \Rightarrow u^2 + u - 4 = 0 [/latex]
[latex] u = \frac{-1+\sqrt{1+16}}{2} = \frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2} = \frac{-1+4.123}{2} = \frac{3.123}{2} = 1.561 [/latex]
[latex] V_G = u + 1 = 2.561 \approx 2.56\text{ V} [/latex]

questions.text:
The ideal BJT in the circuit given below is biased in the active region with a [latex]\beta[/latex] of 100.

questions.solution:
Given [latex]\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}=10 \mu \mathrm{~A}[/latex] and [latex]\beta=100[/latex]

questions.text:
An NMOS transistor operating in the linear region has [latex]I_{D S}[/latex] of [latex]5 \mu \mathrm{A}[/latex] at [latex]V_{D S}[/latex] of [latex]0.1 \mathrm{~V}[/latex]. Keeping [latex]V_{G S}[/latex] constant, the [latex]V_{D S}[/latex] is increased to [latex]1.5 \mathrm{~V}[/latex].
Given that [latex]\mu_{n} C_{o x} \frac{W}{L}=50 \mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V}^{2}[/latex], the transconductance at the new operating point (in [latex]\mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places) is ________
questions.solution:
For linear region of MOS,
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{D} & =\mu_{n} C_{O X}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)\left[\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) V_{D S}-\frac{1}{2} V_{D S}^{2}\right] \\ 5 \times 10^{-6} & =50 \times 10^{-6}\left[\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) 0.1-\frac{1}{2}(0.1)^{2}\right] \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) 0.1-\frac{1}{2} \times 0.1^{2} \\ 0.1+0.5(0.1)^{2} & =\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) 0.1 \\ 1+0.5(0.1) & =\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) \\ 1.05 \text { volt } & =V_{G S}-V_{T} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Now: [latex]V_{G S} \rightarrow[/latex] fix
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{D S} & =1.5 \\ V_{D S} & >V_{G S}-V_{T} \Rightarrow \mathrm{MOS} \text { is in saturation } \\ g_{m \text { (sat) }} & =\mu_{n} C_{o x}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) \\ & =50 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.05 \\ & =52.5 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{V}=52.5 \mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V} \end{aligned} [/latex]

questions.text: An ideal MOS capacitor (p-type semiconductor) is shown in the figure. The MOS capacitor is under strong inversion with [latex] V_G=2V[/latex]. The corresponding inversion charge density [latex] Q_{IN}[/latex] is [latex] 2.2\mu C/cm^2[/latex]. Assume oxide capacitance per unit area as [latex] C_{OX}=1.7\mu F/cm^2[/latex]. For [latex] V_G=4V[/latex], the value of [latex] Q_{IN}[/latex] is ______[latex] \mu C/cm^2[/latex] (rounded off to one decimal place).

For the transistor [latex]M_{1}[/latex] in the circuit shown in the figure, [latex]\mu_{n} C_{\text{ox}} = 100\:\mu A/V^{2}[/latex] and [latex](W/L)=10[/latex], where [latex]\mu_{n}[/latex] is the mobility of electron, [latex]C_{\text{ox}}[/latex] is the oxide capacitance per unit area , W is the width and L is the length.

The channel length modulation coefficient is ignored. If the gate-to-source voltage [latex]V_{\text{GS}}\text{ is } 1\:V[/latex] to keep the transistor at the edge of saturation, then the threshold voltage of the transistor (rounded off to one decimal place) is _______ V.
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{D S}&=\frac{\mu_{n} C_{O x}}{2} \times \frac{W}{L}\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right)^{2} \\ \text{Given}\qquad V_{G S}&=1 \mathrm{~V} \\ I_{D S}&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{D S}=3-20 \times I_{D S} \\ V_{D S}=3-\frac{20}{2}\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2} \\ V_{D S}=3-10\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
MOSFET operates in saturation if
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{D S} &\geq V_{G S}-V_{T}\\ \text{So, we take},\qquad \quad V_{D S}&=V_{G S}-V_{T} \\ V_{G S}-V_{T}&=3-10\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2} \\ 1-V_{T}&=3-10\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2}\\ \text{Let,}\qquad 1-V_{T} &=x \\ 3-10 x^{2} &=x \\ 10 x^{2}+x-3 x &=0 \\ \text{We get,}\qquad x &=-\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+120}}{20}\\ x &=-\frac{1 \pm 11}{20}\\ \therefore \qquad \quad x&=0.5 \text { and }-0.6\\ x&=0.5\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \quad 1-V_{T} & =0.5 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \quad V_{T} & =0.5 \mathrm{~V} \\ x & =-0.6 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad \quad 1-V_{T} & =-0.6 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad \quad V_{T} & =1.6 \mathrm{~V} \\ \text { But }\qquad \quad V_{G S} & \gt V_{T} \\ \text { or }\qquad \quad V_{T} & \lt V_{G S} \\ \text { i.e., }\qquad \quad V_{T} & \lt 1 \\ \therefore\qquad \quad V_{T} & =0.5 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
For an n-channel silicon [latex]\text{MOSFET}[/latex] with [latex]10\:nm[/latex] gate oxide thickness, the substrate sensitivity [latex]\left ( \partial V_{T}/\partial \left | V_{BS} \right | \right )[/latex] is found to be [latex]50\:mV/V[/latex] at a substrate voltage [latex]\left | V_{BS} \right |=2V[/latex], where [latex]V_{T}[/latex] is the threshold voltage of the [latex]\text{MOSFET}[/latex]. Assume that, [latex]\left | V_{BS} \right | \gg 2\Phi _{B}[/latex], where [latex]q\Phi _{B}[/latex] is the separation between the Fermi energy level [latex]E_{F}[/latex] and the intrinsic level [latex]E_{i}[/latex] in the bulk. Parameters given are
Electron charge [latex](q) = 1.6 \times 101^{-19}\:C[/latex]
Vacuum permittivity [latex](\varepsilon _{0}) = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\: F/m[/latex]
Relative permittivity of silicon [latex](\varepsilon _{Si}) = 12[/latex]
Relative permittivity of oxide [latex](\varepsilon _{ox}) = 4[/latex]
The doping concentration of the substrate is
questions.solution:
Given, N -channel MOSFET
[latex] \begin{aligned} t_{o x}&=10 \mathrm{~nm}=10 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~cm} & \\ \frac{\partial V_{T}}{\partial\left|V_{B S}\right|}&=50 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{V}, & \left|V_{B S}\right|=2 \mathrm{~V} \\ \qquad q&=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C} & \left|V_{B S}\right|>>2 \phi_{B} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \epsilon_{o} &=8.85 \times 10^{-14} \mathrm{~F} / \mathrm{cm} \\ \epsilon_{r_{\mathrm{Si}}} &=12 \\ \epsilon_{r_{O x}} &=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Threshold voltage, including body effect,
[latex] V_{T}=\phi_{m s}+\frac{\sqrt{2 \epsilon_{s i} q N_{A}\left(2 \phi_{B}-V_{B S}\right)}}{C_{o x}}+2 \phi_{B}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{In question, we need, } \left|V_{B S}\right|&=\left|V_{S B}\right| \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad V_{T}&=\phi_{m s}+\frac{\sqrt{2 \epsilon_{s i} q N_{A}\left(2 \phi_{B}+V_{S B}\right)}}{C_{o x}}+2 \phi_{B}\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad V_{T}&=\phi_{m s}+\frac{\sqrt{2 \epsilon_{s i} q N_{A}\left(2 \phi_{B}+\left|V_{S B}\right|\right)}}{C_{O x}}+2 \phi_{B}\\ \therefore \qquad\qquad \frac{\partial V_{T}}{\partial\left|V_{B S}\right|}&=0+\frac{\sqrt{2 \epsilon_{s i} q N_{A}}}{C_{O x}} \cdot \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2 \phi_{B}+\left|V_{S B}\right|}}+0\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad 50 \times 10^{-3}&=\frac{\sqrt{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14} \times 12 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~N}_{A}}}{\epsilon_{\alpha x} / t_{0 x}} \cdot \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\left|V_{S B}\right|}}\\ \left(\frac{50 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14}}{10 \times 10^{-7}}\right)^{2}&=\frac{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14} \times 12 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{4 \times 2}\\ &\left[\because\left|V_{S B}\right| \gt \gt 2 \phi_{B}\right]\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad N_{A}&=7.375 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Both the transistors are biased in the saturation region of operation, but the gate overdrive voltage ([latex]V_{GS}-V_{TH}[/latex]) of T2 is double that of T1, where [latex]V_{GS} \; and \; V_{TH}[/latex] are the gate-to-source voltage and threshold voltage of the transistors, respectively. If the drain current and transconductance of T1 are [latex]I_{D1} \; and \; g_{m1}[/latex] respectively, the corresponding values of these two parameters for T2 are
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} W_{2} &=2 \mathrm{W} \\ V_{\text {GS2 }}-V_{T 2} &=\left(V_{G S 1}-V_{T 1}\right) \\ \frac{I_{D 2}}{I_{D 1}} &=\frac{W_{2}}{W_{1}} \times\left(\frac{V_{G S 2}-V_{T 2}}{V_{G S 1}-V_{T 1}}\right)^{2} \\ &=2 \times 4=8 \\ I_{D 2} &=8 I_{D 1} \\ \frac{g_{m 2}}{g_{m 1}} &=\frac{W_{2}}{W_{1}} \times \frac{V_{G S 2}-V_{T 2}}{V_{G S 1}-V_{T 1}}=2 \times 2=4 \\ g_{m 2} &=4 g_{m 1} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A MOS capacitor is fabricated on p-type Si (silicon) where the metal work function is 4.1 eV and electron affinity of Si is 4.0 eV. [latex]E_{C}-F_{F}[/latex]=0.9 eV, where [latex]E_{C}[/latex] and [latex]E_{F}[/latex] are the conduction band minimum and the Fermi energy levels of Si, respectively. Oxide [latex]\in_{r}=3.9,\in_{o}=8.85 \times 10^{-14}[/latex] F/cm, oxide thickness [latex]t_{ox} = 0.1 \mu m[/latex] and electronic charge [latex] q =1.6 \times 10^{-19} C[/latex]. If the measured flat band voltage of the capacitor is -1V, then the magnitude of the fixed charge at the oxide-semiconductor interface, in [latex]nC/cm^{2}[/latex], is __________.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \theta_{0} &=4.1 \mathrm{eV} \\ e_{K} &=4 \mathrm{eV} \\ E_{C}-E_{F P} &=0.9 \mathrm{eV} \\ e \phi_{s} &=e x+0.9=4.9 \mathrm{eV} \\ \phi_{m} &=4.1 \mathrm{V}, \quad \phi_{s}=4.9 \mathrm{V} \\ \phi_{m s} &=\phi_{m}-\phi_{s}=4.1-4.9=-0.8 \mathrm{v} \\ C_{o x} &=\frac{\epsilon_{O x}}{t_{o x}}=\frac{3.9 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14}}{0.1 \times 10^{-4}}\\ &=34.515 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{F} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \\ V_{F B} &=\phi_{\text {rns }}-\frac{\phi_{o x}^{\prime}}{C_{O x}} \\ \frac{\phi_{O x}^{\prime}}{C_{O x}} &=-0.8+1=0.2 \mathrm{V} \\ \phi_{o x}^{\prime} &=0.2 \times C_{0 x} \\ &=0.2 \times 34.515 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \\ &=6.903 \mathrm{nC} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: An npn bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is operating in the active region. If the reverse bias across the base - collector junction is increased, then
options: the effective base width increases and common - emitter current gain increases
the effective base width increases and common - emitter current gain decreases
the effective base width decreases and common - emitter current gain increases
the effective base width decreases and common -  emitter current gain decreases
questions.solution: When a BJT is in active region, as the reverse  bias voltage across collector-base junction  increased, the width of depletion region increases,  which results in decrease of effective base width.  This decrease in effective base width reduces the  recombinations in base region, hence, common-emitter  current gain will increase.

questions.text: Consider an n-channel MOSFET having width W, length L, electron mobility in the channel [latex]\mu_{n}[/latex] and oxide capacitance per unit area [latex]C_{ox}[/latex]. If gate-to-source voltage [latex]V_{GS}[/latex]=0.7V, drain-tosource voltage [latex]V_{DS}=0.1V,(\mu_{n}C_{ox})=100\mu A/V^{2}[/latex],threshold voltage [latex]V_{TH}=0.3 V [/latex] and (W/L)=50,then the transconductance [latex]g_{m}[/latex](in mA/V) is ___________.
questions.solution:
Given that,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{G S} &=0.7 \mathrm{V}, V_{T H}=0.3 \mathrm{V}, V_{D S}=0.1 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{G S}-V_{T H} &=0.4>V_{D S} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow[/latex] MOSFET is in linear region
In linear region,
[latex] I_{D}=K_{n}\left[2\left(V_{G S}-V_{T H}\right) V_{O S}-V_{D S}^{2}\right][/latex]
Transconductance
[latex] \begin{aligned} g_{m}&=\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{G S}}=2 K_{n} V_{D S} \\ K_{n}&=\frac{K_{n}}{2}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)=\frac{\mu_{n} C_{O x}}{2}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)\\ \text{So,}\quad g_{m} &=2 K_{n} V_{D S}=\mu_{n} C_{O x}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right) V_{D S} \\ &=100 \times 50 \times 0.1 \mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V} \\ &=0.5 \mathrm{mA} N \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: For a narrow base PNP BJT, the excess minority carrier concentration ([latex]\Delta n_{E}[/latex] for emitter, [latex]\Delta p_{E0}[/latex] for base. [latex]\Delta n_{c}[/latex] for collector) normalized to equilibrium minority carrier concentration ([latex] n_{E0}[/latex] for emmiter, [latex] p_{B0} [/latex] for base, [latex]n_{C0}[/latex] for collector) in the quasi-neutral emitter, base and collector regions are shown below. Which one of the following biasing modes is the transistor operating in ?
questions.solution:
Emitter-base junction [latex](J_{E})[/latex] is in RB
Collector-base junction [latex](J_{C})[/latex] is in FB
Hence, inverse active mode.

questions.text: Figures I and II show two MOS capacitors of unit area. The capacitor in Figure I has insulator materials X (of thickness [latex]t_1 = 1[/latex]nm and dielectric constant [latex]\varepsilon _{1}[/latex] = 4) and Y (of thickness [latex]t_2 = 3 [/latex]nm and dielectric constant [latex]\varepsilon _{2}[/latex] = 20). The capacitor in Figure II has only insulator material X of thickness [latex]t_{Eq}[/latex]. If the capacitors are of equal capacitance, then the value of [latex]t_{Eq}[/latex] (in nm) is __________
questions.solution:
From the figure I.
Both the capacitors [latex]C_{1}[/latex] and [latex]C_{2}[/latex] are in series
Total Capacitance, [latex]C=\frac{C_{1} C_{2}}{C_{1}+C_{2}} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} C=& \frac{A e_{1}}{A_{1}} \cdot \frac{A \varepsilon_{2}}{t_{2}} \\ =& \frac{A x_{1}+A \varepsilon_{2}}{t_{1}}+\frac{A \times 20}{12} \\ =& \frac{10^{-9} \cdot \frac{A \times 10^{-9}}{4 \times 4}+\frac{A \times 20}{3 \times 10^{-9}}}{10^{-9}} \\ C=& 2.5 \times 10^{9} \times A \end{aligned}[/latex]
From figure II
[latex] C=\frac{\varepsilon A}{t_{\theta q}}[/latex]
since both capacitors must be equal in figures I and II
[latex] \begin{array}{r} 2.5 \times 10^{9} \times A=\frac{A \times 4}{t_{e q}} \\ t_{e q}=1.6 \mathrm{nm} \end{array}[/latex]

questions.text: The injected excess electron concentration profile in the base region of an npn BJT, biased in the active region, is linear, as shown in the figure. If the area of the emitter-base junction is 0.001 [latex]cm^{2},\mu _{n}=800 cm^{2}/(V-s)[/latex] in the base region and depletion layer widths are negligible, then the collector current [latex]I_{C}[/latex] (in mA) at room temperature is __________ (Given: thermal voltage [latex]V_{T}[/latex] = 26 mV at room temperature, electronic charge [latex]q=1.6\times 10^{-19}C[/latex])
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} I_{c} &=A q D_{n} \frac{d n}{d x} \text { where } D_{n}=\mu_{n} V_{T} \\ &=0.001\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right) 800 \times 26 \times 10^{-3}\left[\frac{10^{14}}{0.5 \times 10^{-4}}\right] \\ &=66.56 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{A}=6.656 \mathrm{mA} \end{aligned}[/latex]
