questions.text: If [latex]\vec{E}=-9(2y^{3}-3yz^{2})\hat{x}-(6xy^{2}-3xz^{2})\hat{y}+(6xyz)\hat{z}[/latex] is the electric field in a source free region, a valid expression for the electrostatic potential is
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} E &=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \hat{a}_{x}-\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \hat{a}_{y}-\frac{\partial V}{\partial Z} \hat{a}_{z} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} &=2 y^{3}-3 y z^{2} &V=2 x y^{3}-3 x y z^{2}+K_{1} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} &=6 x y^{2}-3 x z^{2} &V=2 x y^{3}-3 x y z^{2}+K_{2} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} &=-6 x y z &V=-3 x y z^{2}+K_{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Comparing all three for uniqueness solution of potential
[latex] \begin{array}{c} K_{1}=K_{2}=0, \quad K_{3}=2 x y^{3} \\ \vec{E}=-\left(2 y^{3}-3 y z^{2}\right) \hat{x}-\left(6 x y^{2}-3 x z^{2}\right) \hat{y}+(6 x y z) \hat{z} \end{array}[/latex]
as we know that [latex]E=-\nabla V [/latex]
[latex] E=-\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \hat{x}+\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \hat{y}+\frac{\partial}{\partial z} \hat{z}\right) V \quad\ldots(i)[/latex]
Clearly option (D) satisfies the given relation.

questions.text: The electric field (assumed to be one-dimensional) between two points A and B is shown. Let [latex]\psi _{A}[/latex] and [latex]\psi _{B}[/latex] be the electrostatic potentials at A and B, respectively. The value of [latex]\psi _{B}-\psi _{A}[/latex] in Volts is
questions.solution:
E is linear from A to B and E=mx+C
[latex] \begin{aligned} V&=-\int_{B}^{A}(m x+c) d x \\ \text { At point } A: x&= 0, E=c=2 \times 10^{6} \vee / m =x 10^{-6}\\ \text { At point } B: x &=5 \times 10^{-6} \\ E &=4 \times 10^{6}=m \times 5 \times 10^{-6}+2 \times 10^{6} \\ m &=4 \times 10^{11}\\ -\int^{\Psi_{A}}_{\Psi_{B}} E \cdot d l&=-\int_{5\mu m}^{0}\left[20 \times 10^{5} \times 5 \times 10^{-6}+\frac{4 \times 10^{11}}{2}\left[\left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)-0^{2}\right]\right] \\ \Psi_{A}-\Psi_{B} &=-\left[\left(20 \times 10^{5} \times 5 \times 10^{-6}\right)+\frac{4 \times 10^{11}}{2}\left[\left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)^{2}-0^{2}\right]\right] \\ &=-\left[10+\left(2 \times 10^{11} \times 25 \times 10^{-12}\right)\right] \\ &=-15 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A region shown below contains a perfect conducting half-space and air. The surface current [latex]\vec{K}_{s}[/latex] on the surface of the perfect conductor is [latex]\hat{K}_{s}=\hat{x}_{2}[/latex] amperes per meter. The tangential [latex]\vec{H}[/latex] field in the air just above the perfect conductor is
questions.solution:
since, we know from the property of magnetic boundary conditions i.e.
[latex] \vec{H}_{t 2}-\vec{H}_{t 1}=\hat{K}_{s} \times a_{N}[/latex]
In the given question the tangential field [latex]\vec{H}[/latex] in the air just above the perfect conductor is asked with H=0 inside the conductor
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \vec{H}_{t 1}=0 \\ \vec{H}_{t 2}=\hat{x} 2 \times \hat{y} \\ \vec{H}_{t 2}=\hat{z} 2 \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{m} \end{array}[/latex]

questions.text: The force on a point charge [latex]+q[/latex] kept at a distance d from the surface of an infinite grounded metal plate in a medium of permittivity [latex]\varepsilon[/latex]  is

An infinitely long uniform solid wire of radius a carries a uniform dc current of density [latex]\longrightarrow[/latex].

A hole of radius [latex] b (b \lt a) [/latex] is now drilled along the length of the wire at a distance d from the center of the wire as shown below.

The magnetic field inside the hole is
options: uniform and depends only on d
uniform and depends only on b
uniform and depends on both b and d
questions.solution:
The H field due to entire cylinder without hole.
[latex] H\left(r_{1}\right)=\frac{J r_{1}}{2}[/latex]
The Hfield due to hole only.

questions.text:
An infinitely long uniform solid wire of radius a carries a uniform dc current of density [latex]\longrightarrow[/latex].

The magnetic field at a distance [latex]r[/latex] from the center of the wire is proportional to
options: [latex]r \; for \; r \lt a \; and \; 1/r^{2}\; for \;r \gt a[/latex]
[latex] 0 \; for \; r  \lt  a \; and \; 1 /r \; for \; r  \gt  a [/latex]
[latex] r \; for \; r  \lt  a \; and \; 1 /r \; for \; r  \gt  a [/latex]
[latex]0 \; for\; r \lt a \; and \; 1/r^{2} \;for \; r \gt a[/latex]
questions.solution:
We know that magnetic flux density at a distance r from the wire is,
[latex]\begin{aligned} |B| &=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi r} \\ \text { For } r \lt a \rightarrow I&=J \cdot \pi r^{2} \\ \text { so } \quad |B|&=\frac{\mu_{0} J r}{2}\\ |B| \propto r \text { for } r \lt a \\ \text { for } r \gt a,\quad I&=J \times \pi a^{2} \\ \text { So, } |B|&=\frac{\mu_{0} J \pi a^{2}}{2 \pi r} \\ |B| \propto \frac{1}{r} \text { for } r \gt a \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A current sheet [latex]\bar{J}[/latex] = 10[latex]\hat{u}_{y}[/latex] A/m lies on the dielectric interface [latex]x=0[/latex] between two dielectric media with [latex]\varepsilon _{r1}[/latex]=5, [latex]\mu _{r1}[/latex]=1 in Region-1 [latex] (x \lt 0) [/latex] and [latex]\varepsilon _{r2}[/latex]=5, [latex]\mu _{r2}[/latex]=2 in Region-2 [latex] (x \gt 0)[/latex]. If the magnetic field in Region-1 at [latex]x = 0^{-}[/latex] is [latex]\vec{H}_{1} = 3\hat{u}_{x}[/latex] + 30[latex]\hat{u}_{y}[/latex] A/m. The magnetic field in Region-2 at [latex]x = 0^{+}[/latex] is
questions.solution:
For magnetic field boundary relations are
[latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{B}_{n_{1}} &=\vec{B}_{n_{2}} \\ \text { and } \vec{H}_{t_{1}}-\vec{H}_{t_{2}} &=-\vec{J}_{s} \times \vec{a}_{n} \\ \Rightarrow \quad B_{x_{1}}&=B_{x_{2}}\qquad\text{(x is normal component)}\\ \mu_{1} H_{x_{1}} &=\mu_{2} H_{x 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1 \times 3 &=2 \times H_{x 2} \\ H_{x_{2}} &=1.5 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \vec{H}_{11}-\vec{H}_{t_{2}} &=-10 \hat{u}_{y} \times \hat{u}_{x}=+10 \hat{u}_{z} \\ \vec{H}_{t_{2}} &=H_{t_{1}}-10 \hat{u}_{z} \\ \vec{H}_{t_{2}} &=30 \hat{u}_{y}-10 \hat{u}_{z} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \vec{H}_{2} &=1.5 \hat{u}_{x}+30 \hat{u}_{y}-10 \hat{u}_{z} \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
A magnetic field in air is measured to be
[latex]\vec{B}=B_{0}(\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\hat{y}-\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\hat{x})[/latex]
What current distribution leads to this field ? [Hint : The algebra is trivial in cylindrical coordinates.]
questions.solution:
Applying [latex]\nabla \cdot H=J [/latex]

questions.text: For static electric and magnetic fields in an inhomogeneous source-free medium, which of the following represents the correct form of Maxwell's equations ?
questions.solution:
Intensity - curl - line integral
Density divergence - surface integral
This is order of understanding Maxwell's equations.
For any material
[latex] egin{array}{cc} abla imes E=0 & abla \cdot B=0 \ abla imes H=J & abla \cdot D= ho_{v} \end{array}[/latex]
For source free like charge or current free conditions
[latex] abla imes E=0 \quad abla \cdot B=0[/latex]
[latex] abla imes H=0 \quad abla \cdot D=0[/latex]
If [latex]D=\epsilon[/latex] E and [latex]B=\mu[/latex] H and [latex]\in[/latex] or [latex]\mu[/latex] are constant with distance or direction then
[latex] egin{aligned} abla \cdot(\in E) &=0 & & abla imes rac{B}{\mu}=0 \ abla \cdot E &=0 & & abla imes B=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
These are called as homogeneous/isotropic medium.
For non-homogeneous material. However they are not valid.

questions.text: If C is closed curve enclosing a surface [latex]S[/latex], then the magnetic field intensity [latex]\vec{H}[/latex], the current density [latex]\vec{J}[/latex] and the electric flux density [latex]\vec{D}[/latex] are related by

A medium is divide into regions I and II about x = 0 plane, as shown in the figure below.

An electromagnetic wave with electric field [latex]E_{1}=4\hat{a}_{x}+3\hat{a}_{y}+5\hat{a}_{z}[/latex] is incident normally on the interface from region I . The electric file [latex]E_2[/latex] in region II at the interface is
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{E}_{t_{1}} &=3 \hat{a}_{y}+5 \hat{a}_{z}=\vec{E}_{t_{2}} \\ \vec{D}_{n_{1}} &=\vec{D}_{n_{2}} \\ \epsilon_{2} \vec{E}_{n_{2}} &=\epsilon_{1} \vec{E}_{n_{1}} \\ \vec{E}_{n_{2}} &=\frac{3 \times 4 \hat{a}_{x}}{4}=3 \hat{a}_{x} \\ \therefore \quad \vec{E}_{2} &=\vec{E}_{t_{2}}+\vec{E}_{n_{2}} \\ &=3 \hat{a}_{y}+5 \hat{a}_{z}+3 \hat{a}_{x} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: If the electric field intensity is given by [latex]E = (xu_{x}+yu_{y}+zu_{z})[/latex] volt/m, the potential difference between X(2,0,0) and Y(1,2,3) is
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V &=-\int \vec{E} \cdot \vec{d} \mid \\ &=-\left[\int_{1}^{2} x d x \vec{u}_{x}+\int_{2}^{0} y d y \vec{u}_{y}+\int_{3}^{0} z d z \vec{u}_{z}\right] \\ &=-\left[\left.\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right|_{1} ^{2}+\left.\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right|_{2} ^{0}+\left.\frac{z^{2}}{2}\right|_{3}\right] \\ &=-\frac{1}{2}\left[2^{2}-1^{2}+0^{2}-2^{2}+0^{2}-3^{2}\right] \\ &=-\frac{1}{2} x-10=5 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: Medium 1 has the electrical permittivity [latex]\varepsilon _{1}=1.5\varepsilon _{0}[/latex] farad/m and occupies the region to the left of x = 0 plane. Medium 2 has the electrical permittivity [latex]\varepsilon _{2}=2.5\varepsilon _{0}[/latex] farad/m and occupies the region to the right of x = 0 plane. If [latex]E_{1}[/latex] in medium 1 is [latex]E_{1}[/latex] = [latex](2u_{x}-3u_{y}+1u_{z})[/latex] volt/m, then  [latex]E_{2}[/latex] in medium 2 is
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{E}_{1} &=2 u_{x}-3 u_{y}+1 u_{z} \\ \vec{E}_{1 t} &=-3 u_{y}+u_{z}=E_{2 t} &(x=0 \text { plane}) \\ \vec{E}_{1 n} &=2 u_{x} \\ \vec{D}_{1 n} &=\vec{D}_{2 n}=\epsilon \vec{E} \\ \Rightarrow \epsilon_{1} \vec{E}_{1 n} &=\epsilon_{2} \vec{E}_{2 n} \\ &=1.5 \epsilon_{0} \cdot 2 u_{x}=2.5 \epsilon_{0} \cdot \vec{E}_{2 n} \\ \vec{E}_{2 n} &=\frac{3}{2.5} u_{x}=1.2 u_{x} \\ \vec{E}_{2} &=\vec{E}_{2 t}+\vec{E}_{2 n} \\ \vec{E}_{2} &=-3 u_{y}+u_{z}+1.2 u_{x} \\ &=1.2u_{x}-3.0u_{y}+1.0u_{z} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
The electric field of a monochromatic plane wave travelling in a lossless isotropic and homogenous medium is given by

[latex]\vec{E}(z,t) = E_0[\hat{x}\cos(\omega t - kz) + \hat{y}\sin(\omega t - kz)][/latex]

in a right-handed orthogonal co-ordinate system.

Which of the following is the correct polarization of the electromagnetic wave?
questions.solution:
Given,

[latex] \vec{E}(z,t)=E_0\left[\cos(\omega t-kz)\hat{a}_x+\sin(\omega t-kz)\hat{a}_y\right] [/latex]
At [latex] z=0 [/latex],

[latex] \vec{E}(t)=E_0\cos\omega t , \hat{a}_x + E_0\sin\omega t , \hat{a}_y [/latex]
Here,

[latex] |E_{x0}|=|E_{y0}|=E_0 [/latex]
and the phase difference is,

[latex] |\phi|=90^\circ [/latex]
Therefore, the wave is circularly polarized.

Now, at [latex] t=0 [/latex], [latex] \omega t=0 [/latex],

[latex] \vec{E}=E_0\hat{a}_x [/latex]
At [latex] t=\dfrac{T}{4} [/latex], [latex] \omega t=\dfrac{\pi}{2} [/latex],

[latex] \vec{E}=E_0\hat{a}_y [/latex]
Thus, the electric field rotates from [latex] \hat{a}_x [/latex] toward [latex] \hat{a}_y [/latex] with time.

Hence, it is a Right-handed circularly polarized wave.

questions.text: A uniform plane wave with electric field [latex]\vec{E}(x)=A_{y} \hat{a}_{y} e^{-j \frac{2 \pi x}{3}} \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}[/latex] is travelling in the air (relative permittivity, [latex]\epsilon_{r}=1[/latex] and relative permeability, [latex]\mu_{r}=1[/latex] ) in the [latex]+x[/latex] direction [latex]\left(A_{y}\right.[/latex] is a positive constant, [latex]\hat{a}_{y}[/latex] is the unit vector along the [latex]y[/latex] axis). It is incident normally on an ideal electric conductor (conductivity, [latex]\sigma=\infty[/latex] ) at [latex]x=0[/latex]. The position of the first null of the total magnetic field in the air (measured from [latex]x=0[/latex], in metres) is ________
questions.solution:
At perfect conductor,
[latex] \begin{array}{ll} & \Gamma=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & \Gamma=1 \mid \pi \end{array} [/latex]
As we know that [latex]H_{\min }[/latex] occurs at [latex]E_{\max }[/latex]. Hence,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & E_{\max }=E_{0}[1+|\Gamma|] \\ & H_{\min }=\frac{E_{0}}{\eta}[1-|\Gamma|] \text { at } 2 \beta x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} \end{aligned} [/latex]
So,
[latex] 2 \beta x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{4 \pi}{\lambda} x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\pi[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad x_{\max }=(2 n+1) \frac{\lambda}{4} ; n=0,1,2,3 \ldots [/latex]
So, for [latex]1^{\text {st }}[/latex] value of [latex]x[/latex] for [latex]\mathrm{H}[/latex]-field to be zero is
[latex] x_{\max }=\frac{\lambda}{4} \quad[\text { at } n=0] [/latex]
Now, from the equation given,
[latex] \begin{array}{rlrl} \beta & =\frac{2 \pi}{3} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} & =\frac{2 \pi}{3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \lambda & =3 \end{array} [/latex]
Hence,
[latex] x_{\max }=\frac{3}{4} [/latex]
If the reference is not at interference then [latex]x=-\frac{3}{4}[/latex].

questions.text:
The electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave is

[latex]E=a_{x} C_{1 x} \cos (\omega t-\beta z)+a_{y} C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t-\beta z+\theta) \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{m}[/latex]

Which of the following combination(s) will give rise to a left handed elliptically polarized (LHEP) wave?
questions.solution:
Given, [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x} C_{1 x} \cos (\omega t-\beta z)+\hat{a}_{y} C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t-\beta z+\theta)[/latex]
at [latex]z=0[/latex]
[latex] \vec{E}=C_{1 x} \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t+\theta) \hat{a}_{y} [/latex]
Going by options,

Option (A) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+\pi / 4) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.



Option (B) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=2 \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+\pi / 2) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{x}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=-1 \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.



Option (C) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+2 \cos (\omega t+3 \pi / 2) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \quad \quad \omega t=0, \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is RHEP.



Option (D) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=2 \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+3 \pi / 4) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{x}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.


[latex]\therefore[/latex] Option (A), (B) and (D) are correct.

As we know, wave equation is given by

questions.text:
The magnetic field of a uniform plane wave in vacuum is given by

[latex]\vec{H}(x,y,z,t)=(\hat{a}_x+2\hat{a}_y+b\hat{a}_z) \cos (\omega t+3x-y-z)[/latex]

The value of b is _____
questions.solution:
For uniform plane wave
[latex]\hat{a}_{H}\cdot \hat{a}_{\rho }=0[/latex]
[latex]\hat{a}_{H}[/latex]is unit vector in magnetic field direction [latex]\hat{a}_{\rho }[/latex] is unit vector in power flow direction
[latex]\hat{a}_{H }=\frac{1\hat{a}_{x}+2\hat{a}_{y}+b\hat{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+b^{2}}} [/latex]
[latex]\hat{a}_{\rho }=\frac{-3\hat{a}_{x}+\hat{a}_{y}+\hat{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}}}[/latex]
[latex] \hat{a}_{H}\cdot \hat{a}_{\rho }=0 (\hat{a}_{x}+2\hat{a}_{y}+b\hat{a}_{z})\cdot (-3\hat{a}_{x}+\hat{a}_{y}+\hat{a}_{z})=0[/latex]
[latex] -3+2+b=0[/latex]
[latex] b=1[/latex]

questions.text:
A uniform plane wave traveling in free space and having the electric field
[latex]\vec{E}=(\sqrt{2}\hat{a}_{x}-\hat{a}_{z})cos[6\sqrt{3}\pi \times 10^{8}t-2\pi (x+\sqrt{2}z)]V/m[/latex]
is incident on a dielectric medium (relative permittivity [latex]\gt[/latex]1, relative permeability = 1) as shown in the figure and there is no reflected wave.

The relative permittivity (correct to two decimal places) of the dielectric medium is___________.
questions.solution:
The wave has [latex]E_{i}[/latex] direction and propagation direction both in same plane (ZX).
The wave is plane of incidence (P) polarized.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \beta_{x} &=1, \quad \beta_{2}=\sqrt{2} \\ \tan \theta_{i} &=\frac{\beta_{z}}{\beta_{x}}=\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
No reflection in P polarized wave under Brewster's angle of incidence.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \theta_{i} &=\theta_{B} \\ \tan \theta_{B} &=\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{\epsilon_{r}} \\ \epsilon_{r} &=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The distance (in meters) a wave has to propagate in a medium having a skin depth of 0.1 m so that the amplitude of the wave attenuates by 20 dB, is
questions.solution:
Attenuation constant,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \alpha &=\frac{1}{\text { skin depth }}=10 \mathrm{Np} / \mathrm{m} \\ \text { 20log }_{10}\left(\frac{E_{0}}{E_{x}}\right) &=20 \mathrm{dB} \\ \frac{E_{o}}{E_{x}} &=10 \Rightarrow E_{x}=\frac{E_{0}}{10} \\ E_{x} &=E_{0} e^{-\alpha x}=E_{0} e^{-10 x}=\frac{E_{0}}{10} \\ e^{-10 x} &=\frac{1}{10} \\ x &=\frac{1}{10} \ln (10)=0.23 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
The permittivity of water at optical frequencies is 1.75 [latex]\varepsilon_{0}[/latex]. It is found that an isotropic light source at a distance d under water forms an illuminated circular area of radius 5m, as shown in the figure. The critical angle is [latex]\theta_{c}[/latex].

The value of d (in meter) is _____________
questions.solution:
Critical angle,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \theta_{c} &=\sin ^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_{2}}{\epsilon_{1}}} \\ &=\sin ^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{1.75 \epsilon_{0}}}=49.1^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]


[latex] \begin{aligned} \tan 49.1 &=1.547=\frac{5}{d} \\ \Rightarrow \quad d &=\frac{5}{1.1547}=4.33 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The expression for an electric field in free space is [latex]E=E_{0}=(\hat{x}+\hat{y}+j2\hat{z})e^{-j(\omega t-kx+ky)}[/latex], where  x, y, z represent the spatial coordinates, t represents time, and [latex] \omega[/latex], k are constants. This electric field
options: does not represent a plane wave
represents a circular polarized plane wave propagating normal to the z-axis
represents an elliptically polarized plane wave propagating along x-y plane.
represents a linearly polarized plane wave
questions.solution:
[latex]\vec{E} [/latex] field direction [latex]\Rightarrow\left(\hat{a}_{x}+\hat{a}_{y}+j 2 \hat{a}_{z}\right)[/latex]
Propagation direction [latex]\Rightarrow k \hat{a}_{x}-k \hat{a}_{y} [/latex]
[latex] \vec{E} [/latex] is perpendicular to propagation
[latex] \vec{E} \cdot \vec{P}=0[/latex]
Component in [latex]\hat{a}_{z}[/latex] has magnitude of 2.
Component in X-Y plane has magnitude of [latex]\sqrt{2}.[/latex]
These two components are out of phase by [latex]90^{\circ} [/latex] and have unequal amplitudes. So, it is elliptically polarized wave.

questions.text: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction is mathematically described by which one of the following equations?
questions.solution:
Rate of change of magnetic field results in induced voltage,
[latex] \nabla \times \vec{E}=-\frac{\partial \vec{B}}{\partial t}[/latex]

questions.text: If a right-handed circularly polarized wave is incident normally on a plane perfect conductor, then the reflected wave will be
options: elliptically polarized with a tilt angle of [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex]
questions.solution: Left circularly polarized, due to direction change after the reflection from conductor.

questions.text: Let the electric field vector of a plane electromagnetic wave propagating in a homogenous medium be expressed as [latex]E=\hat{x}E_{x}e^{-j(\omega t-\beta z)}[/latex], where the propagation constant [latex]\beta[/latex] is a function of the angular frequency [latex]\omega[/latex]. Assume that [latex]\beta (\omega)[/latex]  and [latex]E_{x}[/latex] are known and are real. From the information available, which one of the following CANNOT be determined?
options: The type of polarization of the wave.
The group velocity of the wave
The phase velocity of the wave.
The power flux through the z = 0 plane.
questions.solution:
[latex]\beta(\omega) [/latex] is known so [latex] V_{g}[/latex] can be calculated.
[latex] v_{p}=\omega / \beta [/latex] can be calculated.
Polarization can be identified.
[latex] \mu_{r}[/latex] and [latex]\epsilon_{r} [/latex] cannot be found, due to which power flux cannot be calculated as power flux
[latex] P=\frac{1}{2} \frac{|E|^{2}}{\eta}, \text{ where }\eta=120 \pi \times \sqrt{\frac{\mu_{r}}{\epsilon_{r}}}[/latex]

questions.text:
The electric field of a plane wave propagating in a lossless non-magnetic medium is given by the following expression
[latex]E(z,t)=a_{x}5 cos(2\pi \times 10^{9}t+\beta z)+ [/latex] [latex]a_{y} 3 cos(2\pi \times 10^{9}t+\beta z-\pi/2)[/latex]
The type of the polarization is
questions.solution:
[latex]\vec{E}(z, t)=\hat{a}_{x} 5 \cos \left(2 \pi \times 10^{9} t+\beta z\right) [/latex]
[latex] +\hat{a}_{y} 3 \cos \left(2 \pi \times 10^{9} t+\beta z-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow [/latex] Wave is travelling in [latex]-\hat{a}_{z}[/latex] direction.
[latex] \Rightarrow [/latex] Wave has orthogonal components with unequal amplitudes and checking the time trace.
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Wave is left hand elliptically polarized.

questions.text:
The electric field of a uniform plane electromagnetic wave is
[latex]\vec{E}=(\vec{a}_{x}+j4\vec{a}_{y})exp[j(2\pi \times 10^{7}t-0.2z)][/latex]
The polarization of the wave is
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{E}(z, t)=& \hat{a}_{x} 5 \cos \left(2 \pi \times 10^{9} t+\beta z\right) \\ &+\hat{a}_{y} 3 \cos \left(2 \pi \times 10^{9} t+\beta z-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider a uniform plane wave with amplitude [latex](E_{0})[/latex] of 10 V/m and 1.1 GHz frequency travelling in air, and incident normally on a dielectric medium with complex relative permittivity ([latex]\varepsilon_{r}[/latex]) and permeability ([latex]\mu_{r}[/latex]) as shown in the figure.

The magnitude of the transmitted electric field component (in V/m) after it has travelled a distance of 10 cm inside the dielectric region is_________.
questions.solution:
Material has [latex]\mu_{R}[/latex] and [latex]\epsilon_{R}[/latex] complex.
[latex] \eta \text { of material }=\sqrt{\frac{j \omega \mu}{\sigma+j \omega \epsilon}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{o} \mu_{R}}{\epsilon_{o} \epsilon_{R}}}=120 \pi[/latex]
where, [latex]\sigma=0 \quad[/latex] (dielectric)
No reflections at the boundary.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \gamma &=\text { Propagation constant } \\ &=\sqrt{j \omega \mu_{o} \mu_{R}\left(0+j \omega \epsilon_{o} \epsilon_{R}\right)} \\ &=\sqrt{j \omega \mu_{o} \epsilon_{o}(1-j 2)} \\ &=j \omega \sqrt{\mu_{o} \epsilon_{o}}+j 2 \omega \sqrt{\mu_{o} \epsilon_{o}} \\ \alpha &=2 \omega \sqrt{\mu_{o} \epsilon_{o}}=4.6 \frac{1}{\mathrm{m}} \\ |E| &=E_{o} e^{-\alpha z} \text { with } Z=0.1 \mathrm{m} \\ |E| &=0.1 \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
The electric field intensity of a plane wave traveling in free space is given by the following expression
[latex]E(x,t)=a_{y}24\pi cos(\omega t-k_{0}x)(V/m)[/latex]
In this field, consider a square area 10 cm x 10 cm on a plane x + y = 1. The total time-averaged power (in mW) passing through the square area is _______.
questions.solution:
[latex]\vec{E}(x, t)=\hat{a}_{y} 24 \pi \cos \left(\omega t-K_{o} x\right) V / m[/latex]
Power density
[latex] \vec{P}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{|E|^{2}}{\eta}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{(24 \pi)^{2}}{120 \pi} \hat{a}_{x}[/latex]
Time-averaged power
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{\mathrm{avg}} &=\vec{P} \cdot \longrightarrow \\ &=\left[\frac{1}{2} \frac{(24 \pi)^{2}}{120 \pi} \hat{a}_{x}\right] \cdot\left[\frac{\hat{a}_{x}+\hat{a}_{y}}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^{-2}\right] \\ P_{\mathrm{avg}} &=\frac{24 \pi}{\sqrt{2}}=53.29 \mathrm{mW} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The electric field component of a plane wave traveling in a lossless dielectric medium is given by [latex]\vec{E}(z,t)=\hat{a_{y}}2cos(10^{8}t-\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}})V/m[/latex]. The wavelength (in m) for the wave is ___________.
questions.solution:
[latex]\vec{E}(z, t)=\hat{a}_{y} 2 \cos \left(10^{8} t-\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{m} [/latex]
General form of
[latex] \vec{E}(z, t)=\hat{a}_{y} E_{o} \cos (\omega t-\beta z) \vee / m [/latex]
Comparing both, we get [latex] \beta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} [/latex]
since, [latex]\beta=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \lambda=\frac{2 \pi}{\beta}=\frac{2 \pi}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}=2 \sqrt{2} \pi m [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \lambda=8.88 \mathrm{m}[/latex]

questions.text: Assume that a plane wave in air with an electric field [latex]\vec{E}=10cos(\omega t-3x-\sqrt{3}z)\hat{a}_{y} V/m[/latex] is incident on a non-magnetic dielectric slab of relative permittivity 3 which covers the region [latex]z \gt 0[/latex]. The angle of transmission in the dielectric slab is ____degrees.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \beta_{x}&=3, \beta_{z}=\sqrt{3}\text{ from }E_{i} \text{ of the wave}\\ \theta_{i} &=60^{\circ} \\ \frac{\sin 60^{\circ}}{\sin \theta_{t}} &=\sqrt{3} \\ \theta_{t} &=30^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
If the electric field of a plane wave is
[latex]\vec{E}(z,t)=\hat{x}3 cos(\omega t-kz+30^{\circ})[/latex]- [latex]\hat{y}4sin(\omega t-kz+45^{\circ})[/latex] (mV/m),
the polarization state of the plane wave is
questions.solution:
[latex]\vec{E}(z, t)=3 \hat{x} \cos \left(\omega t-k z+30^{\circ}\right)-4 \hat{y} \sin \left(\omega t-k z+45^{\circ}\right)[/latex]
The plane wave is travelling in +z direction
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \hat{E}_{x}=3 \cos \left(\omega t-k z+30^{\circ}\right) \\ \hat{E}_{y}=-4 \sin \left(\omega t-k z+45^{\circ}\right) \end{array}[/latex]
At z=0, tracing E locus for various times

questions.text:
The electric and magnetic fields for a TEM wave of frequency 14 GHz in a homogeneous medium of relative permittivity er and relative permeability [latex]\mu _{r}[/latex]=1 are given by
[latex]\vec{E}=E_{p}e^{j(\omega t-280\pi t)}\hat{u}_{z} V/m [/latex]
[latex] \vec{H}=3e^{j(\omega t-280\pi y)}\hat{u}_{x} V/m[/latex]

Assuming the speed of light in free space to be [latex]3 \times 10^{8}[/latex] m/s, the intrinsic impedance of free space to be 120[latex]\pi[/latex], the relative permittivity [latex]\varepsilon_{r}[/latex] of the medium and the electric field amplitude [latex]E_{p}[/latex] are
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given:}\quad\vec{E}&=E_{p} e^{i(\omega t-280 \pi y)} \hat{u}_{z} V / m\\ \vec{H}&=3 e^{i(\omega t-280 \pi y)} \hat{u}_{x} A / m \\ v&=3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
From given expression we conclude that,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \beta &=280 \pi=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \\ \therefore \quad & \lambda=\frac{1}{140} \text { meter } \\ v &=f \lambda=14 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{1}{140} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{se} \\ v &=1 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \text { but, } \quad v &=\frac{c}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r} \mu_{r}}} \\ \therefore \quad 1 \times 10^{8} &=\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{\sqrt{1 \times \epsilon_{r}}} \\ \therefore \quad \epsilon_{r}&=9\\ \frac{E_{P}}{H_{P}}&=\eta=\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\epsilon}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0} \times 1}{\epsilon_{0} \times 9}}=\frac{1}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\epsilon_{0}}} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{E_{P}}{3}&=\frac{1}{3} \times 120 \pi \\ \therefore \quad E_{P}&=120 \pi \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} H_{i}=& \frac{1}{\eta}\left(\hat{a}_{y} \times \vec{E}_{i}\right) \\ =& \frac{24 \cos }{120 \pi}\left(3 \times 10^{8} t-\beta y\right) \hat{a}_{x} \\ =& \frac{1}{5 \pi} \cos \left(3 \times 10^{8} t-\beta y\right) \hat{a}_{x} \\ \frac{H_{r}}{H_{i}}&=\frac{\eta_{1}-\eta_{2}}{\eta_{1}+\eta_{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\epsilon_{1}}}-\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\epsilon_{2}}}}{\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\epsilon_{1}}}+\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\epsilon_{2}}}} \\ =\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon_{2}}-\sqrt{\epsilon_{1}}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{2}}+\sqrt{\epsilon_{1}}}&=\frac{\sqrt{9}-\sqrt{1}}{\sqrt{9}+\sqrt{1}}=\frac{3-1}{3+1}=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, reflected magnetic field component,
[latex]\vec{H}_{r}=\frac{1}{10 \pi} \cos \left(3 \times 10^{8} t+\beta y\right) \hat{a}_{x}[/latex]
Due to change in propagation direction to -y

questions.text:
A complex load (in [latex]\Omega[/latex]) is represented as [latex]\Gamma_L = 0.5\angle30^\circ[/latex] on the Smith chart. A co-axial cable with a characteristic impedance of [latex]50 \, \Omega[/latex] is connected to the load. The new input impedance of the load now moves to a diametrically opposite point on the same [latex]\Gamma[/latex] circle on the Smith chart.

Which option is the nearest input impedance of the cable connected load (in [latex]\Omega[/latex])?
questions.solution:
Given:
Reflection coefficient of load: [latex] \Gamma_L=0.5\angle30^\circ [/latex]

Characteristic impedance: [latex] Z_0=50\Omega [/latex]

The input impedance moves to the diametrically opposite point on the same Smith chart circle.

On a Smith chart, diametrically opposite point means:
[latex] \Gamma_{in}=0.5\angle(30^\circ+180^\circ) = 0.5\angle210^\circ [/latex]

Step 1: Convert reflection coefficient into rectangular form

[latex] \Gamma_{in} = 0.5(\cos210^\circ+j\sin210^\circ) [/latex]

[latex] = 0.5(-0.866-j0.5) [/latex]

[latex] \Gamma_{in} = -0.433-j0.25 [/latex]

Step 2: Use impedance-reflection coefficient relation

Substituting values,
[latex] Z_{in} = 50\cdot \frac{1+(-0.433-j0.25)} {1-(-0.433-j0.25)} [/latex] [latex] = 50\cdot \frac{0.567-j0.25} {1.433+j0.25} [/latex]

Multiplying numerator and denominator by conjugate:
[latex] Z_{in} = 50\cdot \frac{(0.567-j0.25)(1.433-j0.25)} {(1.433)^2+(0.25)^2} [/latex]

After simplification, [latex] Z_{in} \approx 17.7-j11.8\Omega [/latex]

questions.text:
A [latex]50 \Omega[/latex] lossless transmission line is terminated with a load [latex]\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{L}}[/latex] of [latex](50-\mathrm{j} 75) \Omega[/latex].

If the average incident power on the line is 10 mW , then the average power delivered to the load (in mW , rounded off to one decimal place) is __________ .
questions.solution:
Step 1: Characteristic Impedance Given: [latex] Z_0 = 50\ \Omega [/latex] (lossless line)
[latex] Z_L = 50 - j75\ \Omega [/latex]
Incident power = [latex] P_{\text{inc}} = 10\ \text{mW} [/latex]

Step 2: Reflection Coefficient Reflection coefficient [latex] \Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0} [/latex]
First compute: [latex] Z_L + Z_0 = (50 - j75) + 50 = 100 - j75 [/latex]
[latex] Z_L - Z_0 = (50 - j75) - 50 = -j75 [/latex]

So: [latex] \Gamma = \frac{-j75}{100 - j75} [/latex]
Multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator: [latex] \Gamma = \frac{-j75 \cdot (100 + j75)}{(100 - j75)(100 + j75)} [/latex]
Numerator: [latex] -j75(100 + j75) = -j7500 - j^2 75 \cdot 75 = -j7500 + 5625 [/latex]
Denominator: [latex] 100^2 + 75^2 = 10000 + 5625 = 15625 [/latex]
So: [latex] \Gamma = \frac{5625 - j7500}{15625} = 0.36 - j0.48 [/latex]

Step 3: Reflected Power [latex] |\Gamma|^2 = (0.36)^2 + (0.48)^2 = 0.1296 + 0.2304 = 0.36 [/latex]
So, reflected power = [latex] P_{\text{ref}} = |\Gamma|^2 \cdot P_{\text{inc}} = 0.36 \cdot 10 = 3.6\ \text{mW} [/latex]

Step 4: Delivered Power [latex] P_{\text{delivered}} = P_{\text{inc}} - P_{\text{ref}} = 10 - 3.6 = \boxed{6.4\ \text{mW}} [/latex]

questions.text: A lossless transmission line with characteristic impedance [latex]Z_{0}=50 \Omega[/latex] is terminated with an unknown load. questions.text: The following circuit(s) representing a lumped element equivalent of an infinitesimal section of a transmission line is/are

The standing wave ratio on a [latex]50 \Omega[/latex] lossless transmission line terminated in an unknown load impedance is found to be 2.0. The distance between successive voltage minima is [latex]30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] and the first minimum is located at [latex]10 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] from the load. [latex]Z_{L}[/latex] can be replaced by an equivalent length [latex]l_{m}[/latex] and terminating resistance [latex]R_{m}[/latex] of the same line. The value of [latex]R_{m}[/latex] and [latex]l_{m}[/latex], respectively, are
questions.solution:
Given [latex]S=2, Z_{\min }=10 \mathrm{~cm}, Z_{0}=50 \Omega[/latex]
As we know that, [latex]\quad|\Gamma|=\frac{S-1}{S+1}=\frac{2-1}{2+1}=\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
Now, distance between successive voltage minima [latex]=30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\lambda}{2}=30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \lambda=60 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]

Also, for minima,
[latex] 2 \beta Z_{\min }=(2 n+1) \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]

At [latex]n=0,1 \mathrm{st}[/latex] minima, [latex]Z_{\text {min }}=10 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{4 \pi}{\lambda} Z_{\min }=\pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{4 \pi}{60} * 10=\pi+\theta_{\Gamma}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2 \pi}{3}-\pi=\theta_{\Gamma}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \theta_{\Gamma}=\frac{-\pi}{3} \quad \therefore \Gamma=\frac{1}{3} \angle-60^{\circ}[/latex]

Now, [latex] \Gamma=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}} [/latex]


[latex]\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow \quad & Z_{L}=Z_{0}\left[\frac{1+\Gamma}{1-\Gamma}\right] \\ \Rightarrow & Z_{L}=50\left[\frac{1+0.33 e^{-j \frac{\pi}{3}}}{1-0.33 e^{-j \frac{\pi}{3}}}\right]\end{array}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad Z_{L}=67.97 \angle-32.67^{\circ}[/latex]
Now [latex]Z_{\text {in }}=Z_{0}\left[\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{0} \tan \beta l}{Z_{0}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right][/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad Z_{\text {in }}=50\left[\frac{R_{m}+j 50 \tan \beta l_{m}}{50+j R_{m} \tan \beta l_{m}}\right][/latex]
Here, [latex]\quad Z_{\text {in }}=Z_{L}=67.97 \angle-32.67^{\circ}[/latex]
Going through options,
[latex]\left.\begin{array}{l}R_{m}=100 \Omega \text { and } L_{m}=5 \mathrm{~cm} \\ R_{m}=25 \Omega \text { and } L_{m}=20 \mathrm{~cm}\end{array}\right\}[/latex] satisfy this identity, hence option (B) and (C) are correct.

questions.text: A lossy transmission line has resistance per unit length R = 0.05 [latex]\Omega [/latex] /m. The line is distortionless and has characteristic impedance of 50 [latex]\Omega [/latex]. The attenuation constant (in Np/m, correct to three decimal places) of the line is _______.
questions.solution:
For a distortionless transmission line,
[latex] \frac{L}{R}=\frac{C}{G}[/latex]
Propagation constant,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \gamma &=\alpha+j \beta=\sqrt{(R+j \omega L)(G+j \omega C)} \\ &=\sqrt{R G}\left(1+j \omega \frac{L}{R}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Attenuation constant,
[latex] \alpha=\sqrt{R G}[/latex]
Characteristic impedance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{0} &=\sqrt{\frac{(R+j \omega L)}{(G+j \omega C)}}=\sqrt{\frac{R}{G}} \\ \sqrt{G} &=\frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}} \\ \text{So,}\quad\alpha &=\sqrt{R} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}}=\frac{R}{Z_{0}} \\ &=\frac{0.05}{50}=\frac{0.01}{10}=0.001 \mathrm{Np} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A two - wire transmission line terminates in a television set. The VSWR measured on the line is 5.8. The percentage of power that is reflected from the television set is ______________
questions.solution:
Given that, VSWR (or) [latex]s=5.8 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} s &=\frac{1+|\Gamma|}{1-|\Gamma|}=5.8 \\ \Gamma &=\text { Reflection coefficient of } \\ &\quad \text { television set } \\ \Gamma &=\frac{s-1}{s+1}=\frac{4.8}{6.8}=0.70588 \\ \frac{P_{\text {reflected }}}{P_{\text {incident }}} &=\Gamma^{2}=0.4983 \text { or } 49.83 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The voltage of an electromagnetic wave propagating in a coaxial cable with uniform characteristic impedance is [latex]V(\iota )=e^{-y \iota +j\omega t}[/latex] volts, Where [latex]\iota [/latex] is the distance along the length of the cable in meters.  [latex] \gamma =(0.1+j40)m^{-1} [/latex] is the complex propagation constant, and [latex] \omega = 2\pi \times 10^{9} rad/ s[/latex]  is the angular frequency. The absolute value of the attenuation in the cable in dB/meter is __________.
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V(l) &=V_{O} e^{-\alpha l} e^{-j\beta l} e^{j\omega t} \\ \text { Attenuation } &=\frac{\mid \text { Input } \mid}{\mid \text { Output } \mid}=\frac{\left|V_{O}(0)\right|}{\left|V_{o}(l)\right|} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Attenuation per meter [latex]=\frac{\left|V_{0}\right|}{\left|V_{0}(1 \mathrm{m})\right|}=e^{\alpha} [/latex]
Attenuation in [latex]\mathrm{dB} / \mathrm{m}=\left(20 \log e^{\alpha}\right) \mathrm{dB} / \mathrm{m} [/latex]
[latex] =20(0.1) \log e=0.868 \mathrm{dB} / \mathrm{m}[/latex]

options: [latex]L=250\mu H/m, C=0.2 \mu F/m,[/latex] [latex] R=50\Omega /m, G=0.04 S/m[/latex]
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \gamma &=\sqrt{(R+j \omega L)(G+j \omega C)} \\ Z_{0} &=\sqrt{\frac{R+j \omega L}{G+j \omega C}} \\ \gamma \cdot Z_{0}=R+j \omega L =&(2+j 5)(50+j 0)=100+j 250 \\ R &=100 \Omega / m \\ L &=\frac{250}{\omega}=\frac{250}{10^{6}}=250 \mu \mathrm{H} / \mathrm{m} \\ \frac{\gamma}{Z_{0}}=\frac{2+j 5}{50}=G &+\dot{j \omega C}=0.04+j 0.1 \\ G &=0.04 \mathrm{S} / \mathrm{m} \\ C &=\frac{0.1}{\omega}=\frac{0.1}{10^{6}}=0.1 \mu \mathrm{F} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A coaxial capacitor of inner radius 1 mm and outer radius 5 mm has a capacitance per unit length of 172 pF/m. If the ratio of outer radius to inner radius is doubled, the capacitance per unit length (in pF/m) is ________.
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} C &=\frac{2 \pi \in}{ln \frac{b}{a}} \\ 172 \times 10^{-12} &=\frac{2 \pi \epsilon}{ln 5} \\ & \in \frac{172 \times 10^{-12} \times ln 5}{2 \pi} \end{aligned}[/latex]
If ratio of [latex]\frac{b}{a} [/latex] is doubled then
[latex] \begin{array}{l} C=\frac{2 \pi \epsilon}{\ln 10}=\frac{2 \pi \times \frac{172 \times 10^{-12} \times \ln 5}{2 \pi}}{\ln 10} \\ C=120.22 \mathrm{pF} \end{array}[/latex]

questions.text: A 200 m long transmission line having parameters shown in the figure is terminated into a load [latex]R_{L}[/latex]. The line is connected to a 400 V source having source resistance [latex]R_{S}[/latex] through a switch, which is closed at t = 0. The transient response of the circuit at the input of the line (z = 0) is also drawn in the figure. The value of [latex]R_{L}[/latex] (in [latex] \Omega [/latex]) is ________.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { At } t&=0 \\ &V_{\text {in }}=400 \times \frac{R_{0}}{R_{0}+R_{s}}=400 \times \frac{50}{200}=100 V \\ \text { At } t&=T_{0} \Gamma_{L} 100 \text { volts reflects }\\ \text { At } t&=2T_{0}\\ V_{\text {in }} &=100+\left(1+\Gamma_{\text {in }}\right) \Gamma_{L} 100=62.5 \\ \Gamma_{\text {in }} &=\frac{R_{s}-R_{o}}{R_{s}+R_{o}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \text { Therefore, } \Gamma_{L} &=-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{R_{L}-50}{R_{L}+50} \\ R_{L} &=30 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: In the following figure, the transmitter [latex]T_{X}[/latex] sends a wideband modulated RF signal via a coaxial cable to the receiver [latex]R_{X}[/latex]. The output impedance [latex]Z_{T}[/latex] of [latex]T_{X}[/latex], the characteristic impedance [latex]Z_{0}[/latex] of the cable and the input impedance [latex]Z_{R}[/latex] of [latex]R_{X}[/latex] are all real.
options: The signal gets distorted if [latex]Z_{R}\neq Z_{0}[/latex], irrespective of the value of [latex]Z_{T}[/latex]
The signal gets distorted if [latex]Z_{T}\neq Z_{0}[/latex], irrespective of the value of [latex]Z_{R}[/latex]
Signal distortion implies impedance mismatch at both ends :[latex]Z_{T}\neq Z_{0}[/latex] and [latex]Z_{R}\neq Z_{0}[/latex]
Impedance mismatches do NOT result in signal distortion but reduce power transfer efficiency
questions.solution:
The signal wave gets distorted if there is any impedance mismatch between the characteristic impedance [latex] Z_{0} [/latex] and the transmitting impedance [latex] Z_{T} [/latex] and [latex] Z_{0} [/latex] and receiving impedance [latex] Z_{R} [/latex]

then only distortion occurs.
As standing waveforms the signal has multi harmonics and hence distortion occurs.

questions.text: In the transmission line shown, the impedance [latex]Z_{in}[/latex] (in ohms) between node A and the ground is _____.
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{\mathrm{in}_{1}} &=Z_{0}\left(\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{0} \tan \beta l}{Z_{0}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right) \\ \beta l &=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \frac{\lambda}{2}=\pi \\ Z_{\mathrm{in}} &=Z_{0}\left(\frac{Z_{L}+j 0}{Z_{0}+j 0}\right) \\ Z_{\mathrm{in}_{1}} &=Z_{L}=50 \Omega \\ \therefore \quad Z_{\mathrm{in}} &=\left(Z_{\mathrm{in}_{1}} \| 100 \Omega\right)=\frac{100 \times 50}{150}=33.3 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
To maximize power transfer, a lossless transmission line is to be matched to a resistive load impedance via a [latex]\lambda/4[/latex] transformer as shown.

The characteristic impedance (in [latex]\Omega[/latex]) of the [latex]\lambda/4[/latex] transformer is ___
questions.solution:
Input impedance for quarter wave transformer is given as,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{\text {in }}&=\frac{Z_{0}^{2}}{Z_{L}} \\ \text { Given: } Z_{\text {in }}&=50 \Omega, \quad Z_{L}=100 \Omega\\ \therefore \quad Z_{0}^{2}&=50 \times 100 \\ Z_{0}&=\sqrt{50 \times 100} \\ Z_{0}&=70.72 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The input impedance of a [latex]\frac{\lambda }{8}[/latex] section of a lossless transmission line of characteristic impedance 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] is found to be real when the other end is terminated by a load [latex]Z_{L}=(R+jX)\Omega[/latex]. If X is  30 [latex]\Omega[/latex], the value of R(in [latex]\Omega[/latex]) is_____.
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{\text {in }}&=Z_{0}\left(\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{o} \tan \beta l}{Z_{o}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right)\\ \text{at }\;l&=\frac{\lambda}{8} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \beta l&=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \frac{\lambda}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ \therefore \quad\tan \frac{\pi}{4}&=1 \\ Z_{\text {in }}&=Z_{o}\left[\frac{Z_{L}+j 50}{Z_{o}+j Z_{L}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given},\quad Z_{L}&=R+j X=R+j 30 \text{ and }Z_{0}=50 \Omega \\ 30 R &=80(50+R) \\ Z_{\text {in }} &=50\left[\frac{R+j 30+j 50}{50+j(R+j 30)}\right] \\ &=50\left[\frac{R+j 80}{(50-30)+j R}\right]=50\left[\frac{R+j 80}{20+j R}\right] \\ &=50\left[\frac{(R+j 80)(20-j R)}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, only real part of [latex]Z_{\text {in }}[/latex] exists, so imaginary
part of [latex]Z_{\text {in }}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad Z_{\text {in }} &=50\left[\frac{20 R+1600 j-j R^{2}+50 R}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\right] \\ \text { Zimaginary } &=0=\frac{1600-R^{2}}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\\ \therefore \quad R^{2} &=1600 \\ R &=40 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: For a parallel plate transmission line, let v be the speed of propagation and Z be the characteristic impedance. Neglecting fringe effects, a reduction of the spacing between the plates by a factor of two results in
options: halving of v and no change in Z
no changes in v and halving of Z
no change in both v and Z
halving of both v and Z
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{0}&=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} \text{ for parallel plate line}\\ \frac{C}{l}&=\frac{\epsilon W}{d} \text{ and } \frac{L}{l}=\frac{\mu d}{W} \\ \text{where}, \quad W&= \text{Width of the line}\\ d &=\text { Separation between the lines } \\ Z_{0} & \propto d \quad (Z_{0}\text{ change by half})\\ \text { Velocity } &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L C}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0} \epsilon_{0}}}=3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\\ &\qquad\text{(No change in V)} \end{aligned}\\[/latex]

[latex] =(2 n+1) \frac{\lambda}{4}=\text { odd multiple } [/latex]

questions.text: A transmission line of characteristic impedance 50[latex]\Omega[/latex] is terminated in a load impedance [latex]Z_{L}[/latex]. The VSWR of the line is measured as 5 and the first of the voltage maxima in the line is observed at a distance of [latex]\frac{\lambda }{4}[/latex] from the load. The value of [latex]Z_{L}[/latex] is
questions.solution:
[latex]\text { VSWR }=5=\frac{1+|\Gamma|}{1-|\Gamma|}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore |\Gamma|=\frac{2}{3} \Rightarrow \Gamma=\pm \frac{2}{3}[/latex]
If maximum is at [latex] \lambda / 4 [/latex] from load then minimum will be at load itself.
For the phase of [latex]\Gamma [/latex]
[latex] 2 \beta x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\theta[/latex]
where [latex]x_{\max }[/latex] is distance of [latex]V_{\max }[/latex] from load.
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2 \cdot \frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \cdot \frac{\lambda}{4}&=\theta \\ \Gamma&=-\frac{2}{3}\\ \text{Now},-\frac{2}{3}&=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{Z_{L}-50}{Z_{L}+50}\\ \Rightarrow Z_{L}&=10 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A transmission line of characteristic impedance 50 W is terminated by a 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] load. When excited by a sinusoidal voltage source at 10 GHz, the phase difference between two points spaced 2 mm apart on the line is found to [latex]\frac{\pi }{4}[/latex] radians. The phase velocity of the wave along the line is
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Phase difference }&=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \text { (path difference) } \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\pi}{4}&=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}\left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right) \\ \therefore \quad &=8 \times 2 \times 10^{-3} \\ &=16 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ f&= 10 \mathrm{GHz}=10 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{Hz} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence the phase velocity of wave along the line is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & v=f \lambda=10 \times 10^{9} \times 16 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \therefore \quad v &=1.6 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: In the circuit shown, all the transmission line sections are lossless. The Voltage Standing Wave Ration(VSWR) on the 60 [latex]\Omega[/latex] line is
questions.solution:
[latex]Z_{\text {in }}=Z_{0}\left(\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{0} \tan \beta l}{Z_{0}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right)[/latex]


Input impedance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{1} &=30\left[\frac{0+j 30 \tan \left(\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}\right)\left(\frac{\lambda}{8}\right)}{30+0}\right] \\ \Rightarrow Z_{1} &=j 30 \\ Z_{2} &=30 \sqrt{2}\left[\frac{30+j 30 \sqrt{2} \tan \left(\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}\right)\left(\frac{\lambda}{4}\right)}{30 \sqrt{2}+j 30 \tan \left(\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}\right)\left(\frac{\lambda}{4}\right)}\right] \\ &=30 \sqrt{2}\left[\frac{\frac{30}{\tan \pi / 2}+j 30 \sqrt{2}}{\frac{30 \sqrt{2}}{\tan \pi / 2}+j 30}\right] \\ &=60 \Omega \\ \text { or, } Z_{2}&=\frac{(30 \sqrt{2})^{2}}{30}=60 \Omega & \end{aligned}[/latex]
Load impedance,
[latex] Z_{L}=Z_{1}+Z_{2}=j 30+6[/latex]
Magnitude of reflection coefficient,
[latex]\begin{aligned} |\Gamma|&=\left|\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}\right|=\left|\frac{60+j 30-60}{60+j 30+60}\right|\\ &=\left|\frac{j 30}{120+j 30}\right|=\mid \frac{j 1}{4+j \mid} \\ &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{16+1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
VSWR on 60 \Omega line,
[latex] \text { VSWR }=\frac{1+|\Gamma|}{1-|\Gamma|}=\frac{1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}}=1.64[/latex]

questions.text: A transmission line has a characteristic impedance of 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and a resistance of 0.1[latex]\Omega[/latex]/m . If the line is distortion less, the attenuation constant(in Np/m) is
questions.solution:

Characteristic impedance,

Attenuation constant,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \alpha &=\sqrt{R G}=\sqrt{R} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}}=\frac{R}{Z_{0}}=\frac{0.1}{50} \\ &=0.002 \mathrm{Np} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A rectangular waveguide of width w and height h has cut-off frequencies for [latex]TE_{10} \; and \;TE_{11}[/latex] modes in the ratio 1:2. The aspect ratio w/h, rounded off to two decimal places, is ___________
questions.solution:

For TE mode
[latex] f_{c10}=\frac{c}{2 w} \quad\ldots(i)[/latex]
and For [latex]TE_{11}[/latex] mode.
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c11} &=\frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\frac{1}{w}^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{h}\right)^{2}} &\ldots(i)\\ &=\frac{c}{2 w} \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}} &\ldots(ii)\\ \text{given}\quad\frac{f_{c10}}{f_{11}} &=\frac{1}{2} &\ldots(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
put (i). (in) in (ii)
[latex] \Rightarrow \frac{\frac{c}{2 w}}{\frac{c}{2 w} \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}}=2[/latex]

questions.text:
The dispersion equation of a waveguide,which relates the wavenumber kto the frequency [latex]\omega[/latex], is

[latex]k(\omega) =(1/c)\sqrt{\omega ^2 -{\omega _0}^2}[/latex]

where the speed of light [latex]c=3 \times 10^8[/latex] m/s, and [latex]\omega_0[/latex] is a constant. If the group velocity is [latex]2 \times 10^8[/latex] m/s, then the phase velocity is
questions.solution:
By definition [latex]v_{p}=\frac{\omega}{\beta}=\frac{\omega}{k} [/latex]
where, [latex]k(\omega)=\left(\frac{1}{c}\right) \sqrt{\omega^{2}-\omega_{0}^{2}} \quad [/latex](given)
[latex] \therefore v_{p}=\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\omega_{0}}{\omega}\right)^{2}}}[/latex]
by definition,
[latex] \begin{aligned} v_{g} &=\frac{d \omega}{d \beta}=\frac{d \omega}{d k} \\ &=\frac{d k}{d \omega}=\frac{1}{c} \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\omega^{2}-\omega_{0}^{2}}} \times 2 \omega \\ \text{or}\quad v_{g} &=c \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\omega_{0}}{\omega}\right)^{2}}\\ \because \quad v_{p} \cdot v_{g} &=c^{2} \\ \therefore \quad v_{p} &=\frac{c^{2}}{v_{g}}=\frac{\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right)^{2}}{2 \times 10^{8}} \\ &=4.5 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: The cutoff frequency of [latex] TE_{01} [/latex] mode of an air filled rectangular waveguide having inner dimensions [latex]a cm \times b cm ( a \gt b)[/latex] is twice that of the dominant [latex] TE_{10}[/latex] mode. When the waveguide is operated at a frequency which is 25% higher than the cutoff frequency of the dominant mode, the guide wavelength is found to be 4 cm. The value of b (in cm, correct to two decimal places) is _______.
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} f_{c(01)}=2 f_{c(10)}=\frac{2 c}{2 a}=\frac{c}{a} \\ \frac{c}{2 b}=\frac{c}{a} \Rightarrow a=2 b \Rightarrow b=\frac{a}{2} \end{array}[/latex]
Operating frequency,
[latex] f=1.25 f_{c(10)}[/latex]
[latex] f_{c(10)}\lt 1.25 f_{c(10)} \lt \left[f_{c(01)}=2 f_{c(10)}\right][/latex]
So, for the given frequency, the waveguide will work in [latex]\mathrm{TE}_{10}[/latex] mode.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { So, } \lambda_{g} &=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{f_{c(10)}}{f}\right)^{2}}} \\ &=\frac{c / f}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{1.25}\right)^{2}}}=\frac{c / f}{0.6} \\ \frac{c}{(1.25) f_{c(10)}(0.6)} &=\lambda_{g}=4 \mathrm{cm} \\ \frac{c}{f_{c(10)}} &=3 \times 10^{-2}=2 a \\ a &=1.5 \mathrm{cm} \\ b &=\frac{a}{2}=0.75 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: Standard air-filled rectangular waveguides of dimensions a = 2.29 cm and b= 1.02 cm are designed for radar applications. It is desired that these waveguides operate only in the dominatnt [latex]TE_{10}[/latex] mode but not higher than 95% of the next higher cutoff frequency. The range of the allowable operating frequency f is.

[latex]a=2.29 \;\mathrm{cm}, b=1.02 \mathrm{cm}[/latex]
Waveguide is operating in [latex](TE _{10})[/latex] dominant mode

[latex] \Rightarrow 25 \% [/latex] above cut-off frequency
[latex] =1.25 \times 6.55 \mathrm{GHz}=8.1875 \mathrm{GHz}[/latex]
Next higher order mode is [latex]\mathrm{TE}_{20}\left(\because a_{2} \gt 2b\right) [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c}\left(T E_{20}\right) &=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{3 \times 10^{10}}{2.29}=13.1 \mathrm{GH}_{2} \\ \Rightarrow 95 \% \text { of } f_{c}\left(\mathrm{TE}_{20}\right) &=0.95 \times 13.1 \\ &=12.445 \mathrm{GHz} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: For a rectangular waveguide of internal dimensions [latex]a \times b(a \gt b)[/latex], the cur-off frequency for the [latex]TE_{11}[/latex] mode is the arithmetic mean of the cut-off frequencies for [latex]TE_{10}[/latex] mode and [latex]TE_{20}[/latex] mode. If a = [latex]\sqrt{5}[/latex] cm, the value of b (in cm) is______.
questions.solution:
Cut-off frequency of a rectangular waveguide is
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m \pi}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{n\pi}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{10}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{20}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text { for } \quad T E_{11} &=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^{2}}+\left(\frac{\pi}{b}\right)^{2} \\ &=\frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ \text { Given, } f_{C T_{11}} &=\frac{f_{C_{I E 10}}+f_{C I E_{20}}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{\frac{c}{2 a}+\frac{c}{a}}{2} \\ \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{1}{2 a}+\frac{1}{a}=\frac{3}{2 a} \\ \left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}&=\frac{9}{4 a^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2} &=\frac{5}{4 a^{2}} \\ b &=\frac{2 a}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2 \times \sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} \\ &=2 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider the Friis' transmission equation [latex]P_R = \frac{P_T G_T G_R \lambda^2}{(4\pi D)^2}[/latex], where [latex]P_R[/latex] and [latex]P_T[/latex] are the received and the transmitted powers, respectively.

[latex]G_T[/latex] and [latex]G_R[/latex] are the gain of transmitting and receiving antennas, respectively, [latex]D[/latex] is the distance between the transmitting and receiving antennas, and [latex]\lambda[/latex] is the wavelength in free space.

Given: [latex]G_T = G_R = 1.0[/latex], [latex]\lambda = 0.30 \text{ m}[/latex] and [latex]P_T = +10 \text{ dBm}[/latex].

Choose the distance ([latex]D[/latex]), in km, from the following options at which the received power, [latex]P_R = -90 \text{ dBm}[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Given:
[latex]G_T=G_R=1[/latex], [latex]\lambda=0.30\text{ m}[/latex], [latex]P_T=+10\text{ dBm}[/latex], [latex]P_R=-90\text{ dBm}[/latex]

Step 1: Power ratio

[latex] \frac{P_R}{P_T} = \frac{-90-10}{10}\text{ dB} = -100\text{ dB} = 10^{-10} [/latex]

Step 2: Friis equation

[latex] \frac{P_R}{P_T} = G_T G_R \left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi D}\right)^2 = 1\times1\times\left(\frac{0.3}{4\pi D}\right)^2 [/latex]

Step 3: Solve for D

[latex] 10^{-10} = \left(\frac{0.3}{4\pi D}\right)^2 [/latex]
[latex] 10^{-5} = \frac{0.3}{4\pi D} [/latex]
[latex] D = \frac{0.3}{4\pi \times 10^{-5}} = \frac{0.3}{4\pi}\times10^5 = \frac{30000}{4\pi}\text{ m} = \frac{30}{4\pi}\text{ km} = \frac{15}{2\pi}\text{ km} [/latex]

questions.text:
Two resistors are connected in a circuit loop of area [latex]5 \mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex], as shown in the figure below. The circuit loop is placed on the [latex]x-y[/latex] plane.

When a time-varying magnetic flux, with fluxdensity [latex]\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{t})=0.5 \mathrm{t}[/latex] (in Tesla), is applied along the positive z-axis, the magnitude of current I (in Amperes, rounded off to two decimal places) in the loop is __________ .
questions.solution:
Given:
Loop area, [latex] A = 5\ \text{m}^2 [/latex]
Magnetic field, [latex] B(t) = 0.5t\ \text{T} [/latex]
Total resistance in the loop = [latex]2\ \Omega + 2\ \Omega = 4\ \Omega[/latex]

We use Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction: [latex] \mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt} [/latex] where [latex] \Phi = B(t) \cdot A [/latex] is the magnetic flux.
So, [latex] \Phi(t) = B(t) \cdot A = 0.5t \cdot 5 = 2.5t [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d\Phi}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(2.5t) = 2.5\ \text{V} [/latex]

So, the induced EMF is: [latex] \mathcal{E} = -2.5\ \text{V} [/latex]
(The negative sign indicates direction, but we are interested in magnitude of current)

Now, using Ohm's Law: [latex] I = \frac{|\mathcal{E}|}{R} = \frac{2.5}{4} = 0.625\ \text{A} [/latex]

questions.text: Consider a narrow band signal, propagating in a lossless dielectric medium [latex]\left(\epsilon_{r}=4, \mu_{r}=1\right)[/latex], with phase velocity [latex]v_{p}[/latex] and group velocity [latex]v_{g}[/latex]. Which of the following statement is true? ( [latex]c[/latex] is the velocity of light in vacuum.)
questions.solution:
Phase velocity, [latex]V_{p}=\frac{\omega}{\beta}=\frac{\omega}{\omega \sqrt{\mu \epsilon}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0} \epsilon_{0}}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{r} \epsilon_{r}}}=\frac{C}{\sqrt{\mu_{r} \epsilon_{r}}}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad V_{p} \lt C[/latex]
Group velocity, [latex]V_{g}=\frac{d \omega}{d \beta}=\frac{V_{p}}{1-\frac{\omega}{V_{p}} \frac{d V_{p}}{d \omega}}[/latex]
Here, [latex]\quad V_{p} \neq f(\omega)[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad V_{g}=V_{p} \lt C[/latex]
Hence, [latex]\quad V_{p} \lt C[/latex]
[latex]\quad \quad V_{g} \lt C[/latex]

questions.text: An optical fiber is kept along the [latex]\hat{z}[/latex] direction. The refractive indices for the electric fields along [latex]\hat{x}[/latex] and [latex]\hat{y}[/latex] directions in the fiber are [latex]n_{x}[/latex]=1.5000 and [latex]n_{y}[/latex]=1.5001, respectively ([latex]n_{x} \neq n_{y}[/latex] due to the imperfection in the fiber cross-section). The free space wavelength of a light wave propagating in the fiber is 1.5[latex]\mu[/latex]m. If the light wave is circularly polarized at the input of the fiber, the minimum propagation distance after which it becomes linearly polarized, in centimeter, is ___________.
questions.solution:
Initially the wave is circularly polarized. So, the initial phase difference between field components in [latex] \hat{a}_{x} [/latex] direction and [latex] \hat{a}_{y} [/latex] direction is [latex] \frac{\pi}{2} [/latex]
To become linearly polarized, the wave must travel a minimum distance, such that, the phase difference at that point between the field components in [latex] \hat{a}_{x} [/latex] direction and [latex] \hat{a}_{y} [/latex] direction is [latex] \pi [/latex]
(i.e., the travel of this minimum distance should provide an additional phase difference of [latex] \pi / 2 [/latex] between [latex] \hat{a}_{x} [/latex] and [latex] \hat{a}_{y} [/latex] field components).
So,
[latex]\begin{aligned} z_{min}k_z&\sim z_{min}k_y=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ z_{min}\left [ \frac{\omega }{V_{px}}\sim \frac{\omega }{V_{py}} \right ]&= \frac{\pi}{2} \\ 2 \pi z_{min}\left [ \frac{f}{c}\sqrt{\varepsilon _{rx}}\sim \frac{f}{c}\sqrt{\varepsilon _{ry}}\right ]&=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ \frac{4 z_{min}}{\lambda _0}[n_x\sim n_y]&=1 \\ z_{min}&=\frac{\lambda _0}{4(n_x\sim n_y)} \\ &=\frac{1.5}{4(1.5\sim 1.5001)}\mu m \\ &= \frac{1.5}{4(0.0001)}\mu m=\frac{1.5}{4}cm\\ z_{min}&=0.375cm \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A radar operating at 5 GHz uses a common antenna for transmission and reception. The antenna has a gain of 150 and is aligned for maximum directional radiation and reception to a target 1 km away having radar cross-section of 3 [latex]m^{2}[/latex]. If it transmits 100 kW, then the received power (in [latex]\mu[/latex]W) is__________
questions.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f&=5 \mathrm{GHz}, G=150, R=1 \mathrm{km} \\ P_{t}&=100 \mathrm{kW}, \sigma=3 \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ P_{r}&= \frac{(G \lambda)^{2} \cdot \sigma}{(4 \pi)^{3} R^{4}} \times P_{t} \\ &=\frac{\left(150 \times \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{5 \times 10^{9}}\right)^{2} \cdot 3}{(4 \pi)^{3} \cdot 10^{12}} \times 10^{5} \\ &=\frac{81 \times 3 \times 10^{5}}{(4 \pi)^{3} \times 10^{12}} \\ &= 1.224 \times 10^{-8}=0.012 \mu \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: A two-port network has scattering parameters given by [latex][S]=\begin{bmatrix} S_{11} &S_{12} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} \end{bmatrix}[/latex].  If the port-2 of the two port is short circuited, the [latex]S_{11}[/latex]  parameter for the resultant one port network is
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} b_{1}=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12} \cdot a_{2} \qquad\ldots(i)\\ b_{2}=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2}\qquad\ldots(ii) \end{array}[/latex]
When output is short, [latex]a_{2}=-b_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} -a_{2} &=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad a_{2} &=\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting in first equation,
[latex] \begin{aligned} b_{1} &=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12}\left(\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}}\right) \\ &=\frac{s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22} a_{1}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21} a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}} &=s_{11}=\frac{s_{11}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.text: In an 8085 system, a PUSH operation requires more clock cycles than a POP operation. Which one of the following options is the correct reason for this?
options: For POP, the data transceivers remain in the same direction as for instruction fetch (memory to processor), whereas for PUSH their direction B174has to be reversed.
Memory write operations are slower than memory read operations in an 8085 based system.
The stack pointer needs to be pre-decremented before writing registers in a PUSH, whereas a POP operation uses the address already in the stack pointer.
Order of registers has to be interchanged for a PUSH operation, whereas POP uses their natural order.
questions.solution: The stack pointer needs to be pre-decremented  before wiriting data into stack. For reading data  from stack, such pre-decrement or pre-increment  operations are not needed, as already stack  pointer indicates the address of stack top from  where the read operation takes place.  Hence, PUSH operation requires more clock  cycles than POP operation.
